data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: Volvo loses £1bn in value as it slashes 2,500 jobs
data.description:
Volvo has announced plans to slash 2,500 jobs after a sharp fall in sales triggered a share price slump that has wiped £1bn from its value.

Shares in the company, which is owned by Chinese group Geely, plunged as much as 31pc after it revealed revenues fell by 23pc in the third quarter.

Volvo announced a 5bn Swedish kronor (£376.4m) cost-cutting plan that will result in around 2,000 job cuts in Sweden and another 500 globally “through natural attrition and by targeted exit packages to employees”.

The car manufacturer warned it may have to take “additional actions” after revenues in China fell by almost 50pc and it was hit by the loss of electric car subsidies in the US.

Volvo issued a profit warning and pulled its annual guidance earlier this month as sales declined.

Hakan Samuelsson, Volvo’s chief executive, said on Friday: “We continue to operate in a very tough environment with strong external challenges: de-globalisation, hypercompetition and climate change.

“The third quarter of 2026 was very disappointing and reflects a year that has become far more challenging than originally anticipated. Our ongoing turnaround plan therefore needs ​a decisive reinforcement.”

Volvo is the latest European car manufacturer to announce sweeping job losses. In July, BMW revealed it would cut 8,000 jobs in an attempt to reduce costs. Earlier this year, Volkswagen said it would cut as many as 100,000 roles out of a total workforce of 650,000. The move is expected to result in the closure of four factories.

Jaguar Land Rover, Britain’s largest car manufacturer, said in September that it would cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years.

Volvo’s revenues in the three months to the end of September slumped to 66.9bn Swedish kronor (£5bn), a 23pc decline from the same period a year earlier.

The car manufacturer also fell to a net loss of 5.7bn kronor (£429.2m) in the third quarter, down from a net profit of 4.5bn kronor (£338.8m) a year earlier.

Volvo, which had bet heavily on electric vehicle sales, said the axing of customer incentives in the US under Donald Trump had dented its revenue.

In 2024, the carmaker scrapped a target of transitioning to selling only electric cars by the end of the decade.

Last month, Volvo said that Mr Samuelsson would leave as chief executive next year, with Klaus Zellmer, the boss of Skoda Auto, due to take up the Volvo chief executive of the Swedish car manufacturer “no later” than October next year.

data.title: Tech stocks fall as Nvidia boss warns of AI funding slowdown
data.description:
More than $1tn (£746bn) was wiped off US tech stocks after the boss of Nvidia warned of an AI funding crunch and Meta spooked investors with its spending plans.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 index slid 3pc in New York on Thursday, erasing an estimated $1.2tn of value, while the S&P fell 1.5pc, as fears grew over the cost of sustaining the AI boom.

Surging oil prices helped fuel the sell-off, with Brent crude rising past $112 per barrel for the first time since May.

The tech rout followed comments from Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, who warned that a “scarcity of capital” was hampering the rollout of AI.

“If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neoclouds is off the charts,” he told CNBC, referring to companies such as Coreweave and Nscale, which offer cloud-based storage to AI companies.

“What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth ... because there’s just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there’s a scarcity of capital.

“The demand for capital is much greater than the availability of capital. That’s going to get solved.”

Investors are becoming increasingly wary about the vast sums Silicon Valley’s tech giant are funnelling into the AI sector.

Meta shares fell as much as 7pc after the company said it needed to raise “hundreds of billions of dollars” in the next years to spend on AI despite shareholder scepticism about the financial benefits.

Documents released alongside its financial results on Wednesday showed Meta had around $825bn of spending commitments under leases and agreements in the next few years.

The group, led by Mark Zuckerberg, also raised the lower bound of its capital expenditure this year from $130bn to $135bn and issued new non-voting stock to fund further AI outlays.

Tesla shares slid 2pc after Elon Musk’s group cut its proposed AI spending from $25bn to $20bn.

SpaceX, which is also led by Mr Musk, declined 7pc. Both groups have surged in recent days after a Tesla and SpaceX merger was proposed by the tech founder.

Despite the slowdown in equity markets, Chat-GPT maker OpenAI is closing in on funding that would value the company at more than $1tn, ahead of its long-awaited IPO.

The AI giant is raising up to $30bn at a $1.25tn valuation, according to CNBC sources, with investors from the UAE leading the funding round.

Middle East fears

Fresh fears about the Middle East conflict deepened Wall Street’s gloom.

Saudi Arabia’s state oil company was forced to evacuate staff from its headquarters amid the threat of renewed attacks from Houthi forces.

Aramco told staff to leave its largest office complex and work from home on Thursday after a warning alarm sounded, the latest sign of strain at the world’s biggest oil-exporting firm.

More than 30,000 Aramco employees work at the Dhahran compound, on Saudi Arabia’s Gulf coastline near Bahrain.

Brent crude climbed 2.5pc on Thursday to $111.60 per barrel, the first time it has risen above $110 since May, as the energy crisis escalates.

The Houthis have ramped up an aggressive campaign of strikes on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, targeting energy and transport infrastructure in a new phase of the war in the Middle East that has renewed fears over global energy supplies.

The strikes also hit Aramco’s Shaybah oil field on Wednesday. However, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said the attack had not affected production.

Aramco was contacted for comment.

data.title: Property giant scraps £1.5bn housing scheme in row with Green-led council
data.description:
A £1.5bn plan to rebuild a shopping centre in south London has been shelved after the borough’s Green-led council demanded more affordable housing.

Landsec said it had decided to “de-prioritise” the Lewisham Shopping Centre redevelopment, which would have created 1,700 new homes and accommodation for hundreds of students.

It blamed opposition from Liam Shrivastava, the Green mayor, who refused to back the plans without more homes for lower-income households, as well as those in “exceptionally challenging” economic conditions.

Beyond new housing, the project, slated to start next year, would have included a new 500-capacity music and arts venue and a rooftop meadow.

The decision to mothball the redevelopment will hit London’s housebuilding industry, which is mired in a construction slump.

Housebuilders are starting to pull out of the capital altogether, citing concerns that it has become uninvestable. Taylor Wimpey, one of Britain’s biggest developers, has said it will stop building new homes in the city.

Jennie Daly, Taylor Wimpey’s chief executive, told The Times earlier this month that building in London was “fundamentally broken” and that the incentive to take on risky developments had “evaporated”.

Berkeley, another major housebuilder, said in recent weeks that it was battling “extreme uncertainty” after authorities delayed or halted plans for thousands of new London homes across different projects.

Rob Perrins, Berkeley’s chief executive, told The Telegraph: “At a time when we should be fighting to attract investment and build more homes, we’re fighting it off. The result is fewer homes, less growth and a worsening housing crisis.”

London is on course to build just 20pc of the Government’s annual homes target of 88,000, according to figures from research firm Molior.

The Lewisham project depended on Landsec gaining control of a former Citibank tower next to the shopping centre. Local news site The Greenwich Wire first reported that the council had decided to drop the plans.

But after the Greens took control of the council in May, Mr Shrivastava said he would not help the developer unless it added more affordable housing.

Of the 1,744 homes planned for the redevelopment, 98 would have been offered to social tenants for rent.

A Landsec spokesman said: “Higher interest rates, increased construction costs and more complex regulations have made development in London increasingly challenging.

“Recent statements from Lewisham Council also make clear that the administration is not able to support the next phase of land assembly needed to unlock delivery without a significant increase in affordable housing. This would require material changes to the masterplan which would prolong the programme.”

The spokesman added: “This position, combined with the exceptionally challenging economic conditions, means that we no longer see a sufficiently certain route to delivery.”

Mr Shrivastava said his administration was “laser focused on delivering genuinely affordable housing”. He added: “I’ve consistently said the level of social rent homes in this scheme needed to increase.”

However, he admitted that conditions for major projects, such as Lewisham, were “simply not favourable right now” and that ministers needed to enact “urgent reform” to revive construction.

data.title: Fashion labels favoured by Princess of Wales hit by cyber attack
data.description:
The parent company of fashion brands favoured by the Princess of Wales has apologised to customers after it was hit by a cyber attack.

The Foschini Group (TFG) London – the fashion group that includes Hobbs and Whistles, whose dresses and coats have often been worn by the Princess – told customers on Tuesday that it had suffered a “cyber security incident”.

The South African retail group said it became aware of the attack affecting its UK business on Sunday.

It said the hack had affected “certain of its IT systems” – specifically its Phase Eight, Hobbs and Whistles brands.

The company said there was no reason to believe customers’ payment information was at risk.

In an email to customers, the company said: “On Sunday 11th October, TFG London identified a cyber security incident affecting some of our IT systems.

“As soon as we identified the incident, we activated our business continuity plan, engaged external cyber security experts and informed relevant authorities. Our investigation is ongoing and we are working hard to get all our systems back up and running as quickly and safely as we can.

“All our stores are open as normal and our teams will be happy to welcome you.”

Orders made on or after Sunday may be delayed, the company warned, but it urged customers not to reorder.

TFG is the latest retailer to suffer a cyber attack, after Asos confirmed a potential data breach after hackers sent a smartphone alert to thousands of its customers.

Asos said last week that the hackers tricked an employee into sharing login details. The hackers gained access to some personal information, including names and contact details. However, it is thought that no payment card information or account passwords were accessed.

TFG first entered the UK market in 2015 by buying Phase Eight and has since added womenswear brands Whistles and Hobbs, homeware brand Inside Story and lifestyle brand White Stuff to its portfolio.

Headquartered in London, the group now employs 3,000 people. Inside Story and White Stuff have not been affected by the cyber attack.

In an email to customers, TFG said it did not believe any payment information had been stolen.

“Importantly, payment processing is carried out by a third-party provider,” the email said. “Based on our investigation so far, we have no reason to believe that payment information is at risk.

“As our investigation continues, we will be working to identify if any sensitive information related to our customers was impacted.

“If we determine that your personal information was affected, you will be directly informed. We do not believe it is necessary to change your account login information at this time.

“We know this news may be unsettling and we’re committed to keeping you updated as we have more information to share.”

data.title: Healey plans £1bn Budget crackdown on online retailers
data.description:
Labour is planning a £1bn crackdown on online retailers to fund cuts to business rates for high-street shops, according to reports.

The chancellor will use his maiden Budget to announce that multibillion-pound online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay will be held liable for collecting tax owed by retailers selling goods on their sites.

The policy, first reported by The Times, is expected to raise up to £1bn for the Treasury by closing a loophole whereby mainly overseas sellers take advantage of lax enforcement to avoid VAT.

During the Makerfield by-election, Andy Burnham pledged to increase the threshold for business rates so that 140,000 small high-street shops would be exempt from the tax altogether, at a cost of around £880m.

He said at the time that he wanted to help family-owned businesses, which were the “heart and soul of this country”, and give them “the chance to thrive”.

A Treasury source told the newspaper that John Healey’s priority was to “protect local family businesses and the high streets we love”.

They added: “That means having the beauticians and white van drivers of our towns at the forefront of his mind as the Budget draws nearer.”

Concerns about foreign retailers evading VAT have grown in recent years, with MPs warning HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) in 2025 that the £5.5bn lost to businesses exploiting weaknesses in the system every year is probably just the “tip of the iceberg”.

The Public Accounts Committee, the group of MPs that scrutinises government spending, has accused HMRC of failing to take tax evasion seriously. Overseas sellers avoid VAT and undercut British businesses by setting up fake companies.

Tens of thousands of British shell companies have been set up by Chinese citizens in recent years, giving them VAT numbers they can use to register as UK sellers on online platforms.

Their accounts are then shut down before payment of VAT is demanded. There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by the marketplaces in which they operate.

Under the new proposal, online marketplaces will be responsible for collecting VAT at the point of sale from all sellers who have a yearly turnover of more than £90,000, according to The Times.

Mr Healey is expected to raise taxes in his first Budget to plug a multibillion-pound black hole caused by the Iran war.

On Monday the Institute for Fiscal Studies said the Chancellor faced a £35bn bill to maintain existing spending policies and to boost defence funding to 3 per cent of GDP by 2030.

On Tuesday, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned Mr Healey against unfunded giveaways to ease cost-of-living pressures.

The IMF also downgraded its outlook for British growth and warned of further price rises and job losses.

While the fund did not issue a direct warning to Britain, it said an urgent need to bring down borrowing meant help with cost-of-living pressures should be used sparingly by all countries.

With the Budget looming on Oct 28, Mr Healey has ruled out increasing capital gains tax to the same level as income tax.

He had been considering equalising the two but will not, for fear it would make Britain less attractive to investors.

The Treasury could still opt for a smaller increase in capital gains tax, which is currently 24 per cent for higher-rate taxpayers on the profits of asset sales, compared with up to 45 per cent for income tax.

A Treasury spokesman told The Telegraph: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Banking meltdown proves we’re sleepwalking into a cashless society
data.description:
We are sleepwalking into a society where money exists in our bank accounts, but access to it is based on little more than hope.

Governments want us to go cashless, but they do not seem to realise that weakening our access to cash is stripping away our freedom. If we cannot access our money when digital systems fail, how much control do we really have over it?

The recent Revolut outage is a timely reminder of why cash still matters. Thousands of customers have reported problems accessing funds and making payments, while Lloyds, Halifax and Bank of Scotland have also experienced disruption. With Revolut serving around 80 million customers, the potential scale of disruption is enormous. 

Reports of wider problems affecting Google Cloud and other online services only reinforce the point: when the digital infrastructure we depend on fails, the consequences can spread far beyond banking.

This is about more than inconvenience. We are placing extraordinary power in the hands of a relatively small number of organisations. A society that cannot function without Google, Amazon or a handful of digital payment platforms is a society with a significant vulnerability. 

A technical fault, power cut, cyberattack or problem affecting a major cloud provider could prevent people from buying food, paying for transport or accessing essential services.

Sweden is already confronting this reality. Once celebrated as a pioneer of the cashless society, it was expected to become almost entirely cashless by 2030. Digital payments became the norm, banks reduced their handling of physical money and many shops stopped accepting cash. Its rapid adoption of digital payments made it a model for the rest of the world. But following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, concerns about blackouts, cyberattacks and sabotage have forced the country to reconsider its approach.

Realising that reliance on an electronic payment system left Sweden vulnerable to blackouts or sabotage, the Riksbank – Sweden’s central bank – urged civilians to keep 1,000 Swedish kronor (£80) per adult at home.

Erik Thedéen, the Riksbank governor, told The Telegraph earlier this year that Sweden was taking the threat of Russian hybrid attacks seriously. The government issued a brochure entitled “If Crisis or War Comes” to every household, advising Swedes to use cash regularly to “strengthen preparedness”.

Britain, meanwhile, seems determined to head in the opposite direction. A customer asking to pay with a £20 note is often considered an inconvenience. More and more shops are refusing to accept cash and customers are expected to rely on cards, phones and banking apps. Anything else and you’re living in the Stone Age.

But cash has one crucial advantage: it doesn’t depend on electricity, an internet connection, a smartphone, a banking app or a foreign third-party payment platform. It works when digital systems don’t.

It also provides a lifeline for older people, vulnerable individuals and those who struggle with digital technology.

Nobody is arguing against digital payments. They are convenient, efficient and an important part of modern life. The argument is against making them the only option. Convenience should never come at the expense of resilience. Businesses should be able to accept digital payments, but essential shops must accept cash.

In July, Sweden’s central bank announced that essential shops such as grocers and pharmacies with staffed checkouts had to accept physical cash. Sweden is waking up to a risk we seem determined to ignore. Perhaps it is time we did the same.

data.title: OpenAI slashes valuation by $150bn
data.description:
OpenAI has cut its valuation by $150bn (£112bn) in a sign of growing investor scepticism about the AI boom.

The Silicon Valley company sought a $1.4tn valuation in talks with investors but reduced the figure to $1.25tn after pushback, according to the Financial Times.

The reduction comes as investors grow more nervous about the cost of sustaining the AI boom.

More than $1tn (£746bn) was wiped off US tech stocks on Thursday after Meta said it needed to raise “hundreds of billions of dollars” to sustain its AI investment. Markets were also unsettled by Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, who warned that a “scarcity of capital” was hampering the rollout of AI.

Fears about the sustainability of the AI boom caused a sell off in Asia on Friday morning. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by as much as 2.3pc and was down more than 4pc on the week. A surge in the price of oil to a five-month high has added to concerns.

Dan Ives, a partner at Yorkville Ives, said he was still betting on the AI revolution to deliver but pointed to economic and geopolitical uncertainty in a note to clients, saying: “This will not be the last jittery moment.

“Oil, a 10-year [US bond yield] at 5pc, the midterms in less than two weeks, the Fed path, and the next headline out of the Middle East or the credit markets can each set off another white knuckle day, and the AI revolution names will be the first thing sold every time on the risk-off move.”

OpenAI is looking to raise $30bn before a stock market listing next year. Sarah Friar, the company’s chief financial officer, told employees in August that the ChatGPT maker “will be a public company in 2027”.

A valuation of $1.25tn would still mark a 47pc increase from the $852bn it was valued at when it secured a record-breaking $122bn in March this year.

OpenAI, which charges subscriptions and offers advertising on its ChatGPT bot, is understood to have begun discussions with investors after they approached the tech giant with proposals last month.

Coatue, an American investment group, and investors from the United Arab Emirates are in discussion to lead the new funding round, according to the Financial Times.

Anthropic, OpenAI’s main competitor, is also preparing for an IPO later this year. The company filed its prospectus confidentially with American regulators in June and is currently engaged in meetings with prospective investors.

However, expectations of its potential valuation are also being tempered. Investors have discussed valuing Anthropic at about $1.5tn, a significant step down from the $2tn that had previously been expected for the November listing.

The mooted downgrade comes as revenue growth slows. Financials shared with investors are said to have shown the company lost $80bn in the first half of this year.

Sam Altman, chief executive of the ChatGPT creator, said last month that “right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public”.

OpenAI declined to comment.

data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”

data.title: China blamed for loss of half a million German factory jobs
data.description:
China has been blamed for the loss of half a million German factory jobs since 2019, as experts have warned that Europe’s manufacturing engine is losing momentum.

German industry shed 496,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute in Dresden, representing a drop of 7.1pc.

Joachim Ragnitz, the managing director at Ifo Dresden, said: “Employment is shrinking in almost all industrial sectors, which is likely a result of declining competitiveness, particularly vis-à-vis China.

“Traditional German core sectors, such as the automotive industry and mechanical engineering, are particularly hard hit.”

The figures follow warnings of a “China shock 2.0” as the world’s second-largest economy pumps out cheap advanced-manufacturing exports that threaten to crush Western industry. China’s trade surplus with Germany has doubled in the last year.

It brings back painful memories of the first shock in the early 2000s, when China unleashed a wave of cheap toys, clothes and manufactured goods into Western economies.

In addition to growing competition from China, the Ifo Institute also blamed vanishing factory jobs on a fresh wave of de-industrialisation triggered by high energy prices and changing demographics.

Europe’s biggest economy has suffered several shocks in recent years, reeling in particular from losing access to cheap Russian gas after the Ukraine war.

As factory jobs have disappeared, hiring in less productive sectors has risen significantly.

The services sector employs 2.2 million more people than in 2019, mainly in health and social care and public administration.

Mr Ragnitz warned that this would spell trouble for the future, as these jobs were unlikely to provide a significant boost to growth.

He said: “The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future.”

Car manufacturers and their suppliers have cut 123,500 jobs since 2019, a plunge of 13pc. Meanwhile, metal products manufacturers cut 115,600 jobs, and mechanical engineering another 64,500.

These three sectors account for 60pc of the job losses.

By contrast, service providers saw strong growth with 391,000 new jobs in healthcare and 357,000 in social services, including nursing homes.

Mr Ragnitz said the country’s ageing population was the key driver of this trend.

Germany has for years had a relatively low fertility rate. It improved briefly for a few years before and during Covid, before plunging again to its current level of 1.3 children per woman.

A fierce backlash against immigration means politicians may struggle to offset such demographic pressures.

Industrial decline has caused job losses in every part of Germany apart from Hamburg. Jobs are also falling faster in the east than in the west, at 8.4pc vs 6.8pc. In Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt, overall employment has even declined.

These are both states where the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is popular, with the hard-Right party winning the largest vote share in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt last month. It also won the state election in Thuringia in 2024.

data.title: Sainsbury’s issues cost of living warning ahead of Budget
data.description:
The boss of Sainsbury’s has warned John Healey against further tax rises on supermarkets that could push up food prices.

Simon Roberts said supermarkets had been hit by levies in previous Budgets, and said higher costs for retailers risk undermining efforts to ease the cost of living.

His intervention comes a week after he joined other retail bosses for talks with Mr Healey, where they pressed for relief from business rates and employment taxes.

Mr Roberts said: “Our focus here is about making sure nothing is going to add inflationary pressures or increase the cost of employing people.”

He said retailers were still grappling with the effect of the higher employers’ National Insurance contributions introduced by Rachel Reeves, which had added to the cost of hiring staff.

Mr Roberts said: “We need to make sure that we’re bringing down costs for customers, and we do that by not adding further taxes or further regulatory impacts to an industry that’s already very heavily taxed.”

His warning comes as hospitality bosses have offered to help create 100,000 jobs for young people in return for tax relief from the Government.

He is the latest retail boss to plead with the Chancellor to not increase the tax burden on the sector.

Mr Roberts welcomed efforts to tackle youth unemployment, pointing to Sainsbury’s commitment to provide 10,000 work experience places.

He said: “We’ve got to work really hard with government to make sure that the conditions are in place, such that businesses like Sainsbury’s and many others are really leaning in to solve the UK employment crisis.”

He also called for further action to protect Britain’s food supplies following a summer of extreme weather.

Mr Roberts said: “We need to improve our UK food resilience. We need to grow and produce more at home. We need to create investment conditions where farmers and manufacturers and producers feel confident to do that.”

He urged the Chancellor to increase tax breaks for farmers investing in reservoirs and irrigation systems, warning that Britain needed to produce more of its own food.

Sainsbury’s made £525m in profits from its day-to-day business during the first half of the year, up 3.6pc.

Sainsbury’s raised its annual profit forecast, and it now expects to make between £1.025bn and £1.065bn over the full year, having previously warned profits could be as low as £965m.

However, sales growth slowed sharply, rising just 1.2pc in the three months to September, compared with 2.3pc in the first.

Shares fell around 3.4pc in morning trading following the results.

Sainsbury’s also reported an overall loss of £164m after taking a £317m hit linked to its decision to sell Argos.

The results follow revelations that Sainsbury’s held merger talks with Morrisons earlier this year before walking away from a potential multibillion-pound deal.

Mr Roberts declined to comment on whether talks could resume, insisting Sainsbury’s was focused on growing its food business.

data.title: Housing loans granted while Burnham was mayor under investigation
data.description:
Housing loans granted while Andy Burnham was Greater Manchester mayor are under investigation by councillors.

More than £1bn was lent to approximately 50 property developers – including three controlled by Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi owner – by a fund managed by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) since 2015.

Councillors have now raised concerns about transparency and said the process to approve the loans was “out of kilter”.

John Leech, the chairman of the GMCA’s overview and scrutiny committee, told the BBC: “We just want to be clear that there is a transparent rather than an opaque process.”

Mr Leech said the approval process had been criticised as “very opaque in the past and that it’s not necessarily been clearly understood why X was successful and Y wasn’t”.

Earlier this month, The Telegraph revealed that the Prime Minister oversaw a £55m taxpayer loan to property companies ultimately controlled by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan, the owner of Manchester City FC, while he was the mayor of Greater Manchester.

The decisions to issue the loans were taken in two meetings in 2017, both of which Mr Burnham chaired, evidencing that he was directly involved in decisions that favoured Abu Dhabi.

The loan scheme came from the Greater Manchester Housing Investment Loan Fund, a pot of taxpayers’ money lent to the region by the central government, on the requirement that it would be used to tackle the housing crisis.

The fund was designed to provide loans for “projects which might otherwise struggle to secure financing”.

“In the case of Abu Dhabi, you would imagine that they wouldn’t have any problem accessing funds from elsewhere as well,” Mr Leech, the Liberal Democrat opposition leader on Manchester city council, said. “And so the process clearly does seem to be out of kilter with what the original stated aims were back in 2015.”

Manchester Life is a joint venture set up in 2014 between Manchester city council and Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).

ADUG was involved in three property developments with Manchester Life partially financed through the GMCA’s loan fund.

ADUG, Sheikh Mansour’s investment vehicle, has repaid the loans with interest, but the rate is not known.

A Manchester Life spokesman previously told The Telegraph that ADUG put its own capital into projects before accessing the loans, and that these loans were repayable external debt financing, commonly used by property developers.

The decisions to approve the loans were taken collectively by GMCA members, rather than by Mr Burnham alone.

The overview and scrutiny committee agreed to stage an inquiry into the loans earlier this year and Mr Leech, who has since been elected chairman, is taking the investigation further.

He said the GMCA had been asked to produce a report about the use of the funds and the committee would question officers in a private meeting.

The committee does not have the power to sanction the mayor, but it can investigate, call witnesses, expose problems and challenge decisions.

Renaker, one of Manchester’s leading property developers, received the majority of the £1bn lent by the fund.

Aubrey Weis, a rival developer, claimed the loans had been unfair subsidies, but in July, the Court of Appeal found there had been “no error of law” in the GMCA’s decision. Aubrey Weis is appealing the decision.

Mr Burnham has repeatedly praised the United Arab Emirates for investment that helped to transform the city, but it has not been clear until now that Sheikh Mansour’s contribution was partly financed by loans from taxpayers’ money.

Louie French, the shadow sports minister, said Mr Burnham had “serious questions to answer” about the loans. “Taxpayers deserve transparency over how this money was awarded,” he said.

A GMCA spokesman said: “The Housing Investment Loan Fund was set up in 2015 with £300m of government funding to encourage, accelerate and unlock the building of new homes. 

“Since then, this funding pot has been lent at commercial rates more than three times over, delivering 11,000 new homes and regenerating brownfield land across the city region, while providing new work for local people and Greater Manchester businesses.

“Decisions to grant loans from the fund are taken publicly. Not a single viable scheme was ever turned down and funds were lent to around 50 different developers.”

They added that the fund was open to all developers, with lending criteria based on parameters set by the Government and developed with external financial experts to reflect due diligence standards in the private sector. 

The spokesman said: “Every penny loaned from the fund is being fully repaid, delivering billions of pounds’ worth of development at no cost to the taxpayer.

“Our share of the interest received on these loans, set to reach £37m by 2028, has gone back into work on our housing priorities, including building decent, affordable homes, launching the country’s first good landlord charter and training new housing enforcement officers to drive up standards for renters.

“We are supporting the scrutiny and oversight committee with their enquiries.”

data.title: ‘Pay me or I’ll kick your face in’: The growing menace of cowboy builders
data.description:
Have you lost money to a rogue builder? Tell us your story at money@telegraph.co.uk*.

When he hired a builder to redo the façade of his new home in Kent, Greg Coates* thought he had done his homework.

He obtained seven quotes, then checked his chosen trader out on Companies House and read online reviews of his work. “He seemed really, really friendly and knew his stuff,” Coates recalls of their first meeting.

But then things quickly soured. The work – which was expected to take a fortnight – began a week late because of the builder being on holiday in Mexico, and the delays kept mounting.

More than a month in, Coates, a 33-year-old engineer who had been researching each step of the process, pointed out that some of the work did not adhere to building regulations. He was fobbed off.

So when the contractor texted to ask for the final chunk of the fees, Coates said that he would pay, minus £1,500 until the parts that weren’t up to code were certified.

“Within about two minutes, he called me up, screaming down the phone,” Coates says. If he didn’t pay within the hour, he said, “I’m going to send the boys round, we’re going to rip everything off the walls. We’re going to tear your house to pieces; I’m going to kick your f------- face in. You’re going to wish you never messed with me.”

At the time, Coates was out and his partner was at home on her own, so “blind panic” was running through his mind. “I was really, really concerned for my partner’s safety.”

The couple had only moved a few months earlier. “The last thing I wanted was for the next 20 years to be tainted by this idea of somebody coming round or this looming threat,” he says. So he transferred the £1,500 and called the police. They gave him a crime reference number and told him to call back if further threats were made.

The £10.3bn cost

Coates is among the half of all British homeowners to have been burnt by cowboy contractors, who set clients back to the tune of £10.3bn in 2024 alone, according to figures from the Federation of Master Builders and the National Centre for Social Research.

In August, the Government launched a voluntary scheme that builders can join to “help people identify and hire trusted traders with confidence”. But critics have noted that similar schemes already exist and that, because it is optional, nothing stops those outside it from continuing to threaten customers without recourse.

In July, James Fuller, a builder, pleaded guilty to harassment without violence and two counts of criminal damage after being accused of causing £164,000 worth of damage to former clients’ home after a dispute over the cost of the renovation.

He was filmed on their roof hurling tiles to the ground, allegedly stole the couple’s dog, and made death threats. After a hearing last month, he is awaiting sentencing.

For most who fall foul of builders’ threats, like Coates, it is easier to give in to financial demands than to face further fallout with people who have access to your home.

Some cowboy builders take on more projects than they can manage at once, using the incomplete status of each job for leverage so that homeowners are backed into a corner. They are forced to either pay up so they’re not trapped in a building site, or hire someone new who can plainly see that a first attempt has gone awry, and will charge extra to step in.

Homeowners also report being asked to front cash outside agreed payment plans to cover builders’ personal costs.

Coates’s builder called back an hour after his tirade to apologise, then suggested that he return to do other jobs in the house – at additional cost.

“I said: ‘You’re not welcome at the property any more; [If you come back] you’ll be trespassing and I’ll call the police.’” The builder never returned.

“In all, I paid about £22,000 for a job that I’ve got no paperwork for,” says Coates.

‘He skipped off with our life savings’

For many, fighting back simply isn’t possible. Cal Dunmore*, 44, was going through cancer treatment and caring for his three-month-old baby when he received a call saying that his builder’s staff wanted to go and watch the heavyweight boxing, and “he needed money to pay them so that they could go out and enjoy themselves”.

Dunmore pointed out that they had agreed a payment plan for taking down a dry-stone wall at his 18th-century property in North Wales, building a retaining wall and backfilling it.

The builder then became extremely aggressive over the phone, Dunmore says. “He was swearing at me and all sorts, and threatening to send people around the house and dismantle the bits of the wall that he had built. He was very threatening.”

He then came to the house demanding money before sending his son to do the same, despite the fact that the work was not yet complete.

Given what he and his wife were navigating in their personal lives, they felt that they were stuck with the builder, despite the damage he had already done to their property.

When the last wheelbarrow was being pushed off the property, he transferred the final part of the £24,000 sum – double what he had been quoted. By the time he’d gone back outside, the wall had fallen.

With what was left of it posing a serious risk, Dunmore contacted his council, which he says wouldn’t get involved. He also went to the platform he had hired the builder through, which he says wanted to work as mediators and have a discussion, but the builder just ignored them.

Dunmore readied himself to go to court before being told that costs were likely to be around £20,000. “How are you supposed to take someone to court when they’ve stolen all your money?”

He feels that laws around limited companies enable bad actors, too. “I could set up a company now and rob a whole bunch of people and then just close the company and set up a new one. And there doesn’t seem to be any laws around it. It seems very cowboy-like,” he says.

Dunmore was forced to hire a secondary contractor, ultimately paying £55,000 in total for a job that was expected to take three months, but lasted five years.

His wife also suffered two miscarriages during that time, which Dunmore believes were the result of the stress they endured. “That guy has literally skipped off with our life savings, and set us back as a family,” he says.

Both Dunmore and Coates are frustrated they can’t speak openly about what has happened for fear of further intimidation. “What stings the most is that I want to warn other people; I want to make his life difficult,” Coates says. “But I have to put mine and my partner’s safety first.”

His situation is far from a one-off, he knows. Yet given the lengths he went to in order to avoid falling into this trap, he admits: “I’m surprised it happened to me.”

*Names have been changed.

data.title: Meta accused of ‘outrageous assault on journalism’ with new AI rules
data.description:
Meta has been accused of an “outrageous assault on journalism” after the tech giant unveiled plans to scrape news websites to train its AI models.

The company, led by Mark Zuckerberg, is introducing new commercial terms that let it deploy bots to scrape news sites.

Under the new terms, which take effect on Oct 30, Meta can crawl any website associated with a business account on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger or WhatsApp.

Any business that does not accept the terms must stop using Meta’s sites for commercial purposes.

News publishers have warned that the move would let the company access large amounts of their journalism without paying. Some are considering closing their accounts.

However, they warned that this could have severe financial consequences because many rely on Facebook for traffic referrals.

Local news outlets would be hit hardest, as up to a third of their audience comes from the social media platform.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian, urged the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to intervene to block the new terms.

Theo Bamber, the NMA chief executive, said: “Meta’s bid to force publishers to allow unrestricted scraping of their websites to power its AI products is an outrageous assault on journalism.

“The changes would hit UK local publishers hardest, as substantial amounts of their referral traffic come from Facebook. It is vital that publishers have a strong presence there to combat the misinformation and disinformation, which plagues Facebook.”

The NMA urged the regulator to use new powers under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 to combat anti-competitive behaviour by tech giants.

Mr Bamber described Meta’s actions as a “shameless land-grab attempt” and “the worst kind of arrogant tech platform bullying”.

News publishers have locked horns with tech giants over concerns that AI developers have hoovered up vast quantities of quality journalism without payment.

At the same time, the rollout of AI chatbots and search summaries is diverting traffic from news sites, directly threatening publishers’ business models.

This year, The Telegraph, the BBC, Sky News, The Guardian and The Financial Times joined forces on a new project to combat unauthorised scraping of news sites.

The Standards for Publisher Usage Rights coalition aims to create technical and licensing standards that let news publishers and AI developers do business.

Publishers, including The New York Times, have filed major lawsuits against companies such as OpenAI and Perplexity over alleged copyright infringement.

Some have also signed licensing deals with AI developers, allowing them to access material in exchange for payment.

The Movement for an Open Web (MOW), a campaign group, has filed a formal complaint with both the CMA and the European Commission, arguing that Meta’s actions are “unfair and exploitative” under competition law.

Tim Cowen, the co-founder of MOW, said: “Meta’s new terms are clearly anti-competitive. Many businesses effectively have no choice but to use Meta’s services, and these conditions would force them to sign away rights to their digital content with no way to opt out.

“The terms go live in a few days, and once they’re in force, the damage will be done – you can’t unscrape that content. Therefore, the CMA must use their interim measures powers to block the introduction of these terms whilst a deeper investigation is undertaken.”

A spokesman for Meta said: “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves.

“It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

The CMA is understood to have met with Meta on Wednesday to discuss the changes. 

A CMA spokesman said: “This is an important issue and we recognise the concerns that have been raised by businesses in the UK. We are engaged in urgent discussions with Meta as we consider our next steps.”

data.title: Putin has ordered ‘General Armageddon’ to smash the bridges of Kyiv. This is why
data.description:
As winter approaches, Vladimir Putin is resorting to the one weapon he has consistently used when his armies fail on the battlefield: terrorising civilians and smashing cities. He has just brought in General Sergei Surovikin – aka “General Armageddon” who flattened the Syrian city of Aleppo, killing thousands of civilians in the process – to do the same to Kyiv.

Putin needs something to change in Ukraine, as the Russian offensive in the Donbas has been in serious trouble for months. Ukrainian forces are pushing back around Pokrovsk and Lyman, while Russian casualties remain extraordinary. President Volodymyr Zelensky has claimed that more than 10,000 Russian soldiers were killed in a single week.

Whether that precise figure is ultimately verified or not, there is no doubt that Putin is paying a staggering price for very limited territorial gains. And now he is running short of men: it is getting difficult to recruit enough volunteer “kontraktniki” contract soldiers to replace the losses.

In theory, Putin could simply launch a mobilisation, which would yield huge numbers of new troops. But the Kremlin knows that another major mobilisation, potentially involving hundreds of thousands of Russians, could be politically explosive. The dictator therefore needs a dramatic change in the military equation before he is forced into a decision that could threaten his grip on power.

His answer is becoming increasingly obvious: if Russia cannot defeat Ukraine’s army, it will try to break the Ukrainian people and nation this winter. This is not a new tactic. Putin supported Bashar al-Assad’s brutal campaign in Syria, where I saw first hand what happened when hospitals, schools and civilian areas became targets for Russian firepower.

The calculation was simple: kill, wound and brutalise enough civilians – make their lives dangerous and horrible enough – and eventually they will demand that their own government ends the war. It failed in Syria. It is likely to fail in Ukraine too.

Kyiv is now under almost relentless attack. There were 18 air raid alerts in the capital on Tuesday alone. Russian missiles and drones are striking deep into the city, damaging civilian infrastructure and even hitting the National Academy of Sciences.

The seven bridges across the Dnipro are obvious targets. Kyiv, like most capital cities, is a major road and rail nexus. If it can be cut in half, that has a paralysing effect on the whole of northern Ukraine: imagine the effect on south eastern England if every bridge in London (including those on the M25) were down.

This is not the behaviour of a man preparing to end his war. It is the behaviour of a dictator preparing his population for a longer one.

The danger is that Putin has identified a vulnerability. Ukraine’s stocks of air-defence munitions are under enormous pressure. High-end interceptor missiles such as the US Patriot are in particularly short supply. Moscow knows this. It is therefore adapting its tactics, moving beyond military targets and increasingly seeking to cripple the infrastructure that allows Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities to function.

This is precisely why the West must understand what Putin is attempting before it is too late. His calculation has always been brutally simple: can Russia outlast its opponent? Putin believes it can.

He has shown an extraordinary willingness to sacrifice Russian soldiers. To the Kremlin, human life is a cheap commodity. Russia has a far larger population than Ukraine and has progressively placed its economy on a war footing. Putin therefore believes that Russia can absorb casualties for longer than Ukraine can stand the punishment and, crucially, for longer than Western governments can maintain public and political support.

That last is the real battle. The question is not simply whether Ukraine can hold Pokrovsk or Lyman. It is whether Britain and Europe have the political stamina to ensure that Ukraine is still standing next year, and the year after that.

I am not convinced that our Government fully understands this. The Prime Minister has explicitly stated that, to him, social security is more important than national security. His priorities are upside down. You cannot deliver social security if you are not secure as a nation.

The West must dramatically increase supplies of air-defence missiles, radars, drones and electronic-warfare systems. But we should also be prepared to consider measures that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago.

If Russia deliberately targets civilian infrastructure on an industrial scale, Nato must consider how its overwhelming air power could be used to protect Ukrainian civilians and critical infrastructure without directly entering the war. That does not necessarily mean declaring a traditional no-fly zone tomorrow. It means seriously examining whether Nato aircraft could help defend defined areas or critical infrastructure in extremis, particularly where the alternative is allowing Russian missiles and drones to slaughter civilians with impunity.

The Geneva Conventions are clear: the proper laws of war – not overblown human rights rules, but the regular laws of war – forbid deliberate targeting of civilians without any military purpose. Just when Ukraine appears to be gaining momentum on the battlefield, Putin is attempting to move the war on to ground where he believes Russia has the advantage: a test of civilian endurance.

We must not let him.

Ukraine’s army is fighting back in the Donbas. Its soldiers are inflicting enormous losses on the Russian military. This is precisely the moment when the West should be leaning forward, not stepping back. Putin understands strength, but understands weakness even better.

If we allow him to discover that bombing Kyiv works, he will do more of it. If, instead, Britain and Europe demonstrate that Ukraine’s cities will be defended, its people will be supported and its army will be supplied for as long as necessary, Putin may finally understand the one thing he has so far refused to accept: Russia cannot bomb and meat-grind its way to victory.

data.title: Job fears as ‘vulture’ funds circle struggling rail-freight giant
data.description:
A struggling rail-freight business is being circled by dozens of private investment funds, stoking fears that it could be broken up.

DB Cargo UK, which operates more than 200 locomotives, has been put up for sale by Deutsche Bahn, its German owner, attracting interest from more than 40 potential bidders and investors.

However, unions fear that the business is unlikely to be sold to a single buyer and could be carved up, putting 2,300 jobs in doubt.

An industry source said it was “likely the bids will be from vulture capitalists”.

Aslef, which represents the firm’s 650 train drivers, said management had disclosed the interest from private funds in a document provided to staff.

The union said in its October newsletter that the document posed the question: “What happens if a buyer cannot be found?”

The company answered that it was “too early to speculate but we are currently talking to more than 40 debt and equity providers”.

James Glew, an Aslef official at DB Cargo, said: “The problem with this, from our point of view, is who they may sell the company to and what their intentions may or may not be.

“Everyone hopes the company will be acquired by someone who wants to run it as a going concern. But what for the future if it is acquired by an asset-stripping company?”

A source close to the sales process said a number of bids had also been received for the group as a whole.

The break-up fears have been compounded by DB Cargo UK’s poor financial performance in recent years.

The business owns dozens of potentially valuable brownfield sites across Britain, including 150 depots, terminals and railheads. Many are on the edges of urban areas and ripe for housing development.

Aslef said there were also concerns that DB Cargo’s fleet of 228 locomotives and 6,500 wagons could be sold abroad or even for scrap.

Simon Weller, Aslef’s assistant general secretary, claimed at the Trades Union Congress conference last month that Deutsche Bahn appeared intent on a “fire sale” of the UK business.

He said: “There is a lot of land up for sale. There is a huge amount of money in this sale in redevelopment.”

The Transport Salaried Staffs’ Association, which represents technical and office staff and managers at DB Cargo, said Deutsche Bahn had failed to rule out compulsory redundancies.

The Government has previously said it plans to expand the rail-freight sector 75pc by 2050 as it seeks to shift more cargo from road to rail.

DB Cargo was the dominant player in the rail-freight sector at the time of its privatisation in 1995, when it was known as English, Welsh & Scottish Railway, with a 90pc market share.

Deutsche Bahn bought the business for £309m in 2007. However, Britain’s industrial decline and the decision to close coal-fired power stations led to a slump in cargo volumes.

The UK arm had a £12m loss in 2024, down from £68m in 2023. Its market share dropped to 22pc in the three months through June, the lowest since records began, behind GB Railfreight and Freightliner.

A spokesman for Deutsche Bahn said the divestment process for DB Cargo UK was ongoing and that it could not comment further.

Interpath, which is advising on the auction, also declined to comment.

data.title: Great British Railways chairman to earn £250k – without any rail experience
data.description:
A banking executive will become the chairman of Labour’s Great British Railways (GBR) quango on a £250,000 salary – despite never having worked in the rail industry.

Sir John Kingman, the chairman of Barclays Bank UK, took up the post on Friday with a brief to shape the new organisation.

GBR is being set up by Labour’s Railways Bill to oversee Britain’s entire rail network, integrating track management with passenger train operations. It will be the UK’s third-largest public sector organisation, behind the NHS and the military.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, said Sir John had an “exceptional record” and added that the appointment was a “defining moment in our mission to put passengers first and rebuild Britain’s railways”.

However, the decision to appoint someone with no transport background to such a sensitive post will fuel the growing controversy over the new quango.

Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform UK, said the appointment was a “civil service stitch-up”.

Richard Holden, the shadow transport secretary, previously warned that GBR would be a costly monopoly undermining competition and passenger choice, whose sheer size would make it unaccountable.

Sir John’s appointment was the latest step in setting up the quango, after the site of its headquarters in Becketwell, Derby, was revealed last week.

However, the organisation will only be formally established once the Railways Bill is approved, which is expected to take another year.

It means the existing state-owned organisations that it will replace – track managers Network Rail and DfT Operator Ltd (Dfto), which oversees 10 train operating companies – will remain in situ.

Their chairmen – both also appointed earlier this year – will also stay on so taxpayers will be funding the salaries of all three overlapping roles for at least a year.

Richard George, Network Rail’s chairman, is paid £315,000 a year, while Sir Andrew Haines, Dfto’s chairman and the former boss of Network Rail, gets £160,000 a year.

Sir John, a former Treasury mandarin, will also retain his existing job as non-executive chairman of Barclays Bank UK, for which he was paid £600,000 last year. Barclays recently extended his term by another three years.

Sir John’s early career includes a spell as a columnist for the Financial Times. He also worked in the chief executive’s office at BP from 1997 to 1998, later rising to become a permanent secretary at the Treasury. There, he played a central role in the UK government’s response to the 2008 financial crisis, including the nationalisation of Northern Rock.

Sir John said: “The opportunity to lead Great British Railways is one I could not let pass. It is a privilege to be involved in rail’s next chapter making sure that public ownership of the railways delivers change that people can see.

“I want to help to build a simpler, more unified railway that puts the interests of the passengers and customers first, supports growth and creates opportunity across the country.”

However, opponents of the GBR plan were critical. Mr Tice said: “A fat cat with zero rail industry experience is made chair of the new railways quango on a massive salary. It’s another fine stitch-up from the civil service.”
