data.title: How Labour’s nationalising of South Western Railway made things worse
data.description:
Davor Palic has become wearily used to leaving ridiculously early for work. The 38-year-old estate agent lives in Woking, regularly taking the recently nationalised South Western Railway (SWR) service to London Waterloo. But he’s developed a fairly simple rule of thumb over the years: if he needs to be somewhere on time, he probably shouldn’t trust the SWR timetable.

“Sometimes it’s delayed more than 30 minutes,” he says, shaking his head. “Usually it’s five or seven minutes, but even that’s enough to make me miss the bus at the other end. It’s annoying because I can be late for work a lot.”

And even when the train is on time, Palic says it can sometimes arrive at one of the busiest stations on the South Western Railway network with just five carriages rather than the full advertised length of up to 12.

“In the morning it’s so busy,” Palic explains. “It makes the overcrowding worse and it’s very hard to get a seat.”

It wasn’t meant to be this way. When Labour brought SWR into public ownership in May 2025 – the first operator to be taken in-house by the Labour Government – Heidi Alexander, the Secretary of State for Transport, promised a “cultural reset” for the railway, a “new dawn moving away from 30 years of inefficiency, delayed services and failing passengers, and moving confidently into a new era – the era of Great British Railways”.

A year down the line on June 11, 2026, Alexander was forced to accept in the House of Commons that performance at South Western Railway had “not been up to scratch”. She promised, as many have before her, to “leave no stone unturned” to improve the travel experience in future.

What’s happened since, though, is even more worrying for the likes of Eileen Taylor, 81. She travels on the line every week with her husband. “It has actually got worse with delays and timetabling,” she points out. “Someone told me they’d been standing for three hours on a service recently.”

All of which isn’t just anecdotal, it’s a failure of a nationalisation project borne out by facts published by SWR itself.

In the latest four-week performance period, only 65.34 per cent of its services arrived on time. In the quarter before nationalisation this figure was at 67.8 per cent. On the main line – the routes carrying passengers between places such as Woking, Guildford and Waterloo – the figure is just 50.98 per cent.

Even if you use the industry’s more forgiving measure of a train arriving within three minutes of schedule, SWR achieved 81.78 per cent across the network and just 68.86 per cent on the main line. Again, in the quarter before nationalisation it was empirically better, at 85.7 per cent.

It’s only when that measure is extended by up to a 15-minute delay that the figures rise above 90 per cent, tallying with Palic’s experience of regular small delays, and causing SWR to miss its punctuality targets.

So much for improving the experience of passengers. Jeremy Varns from campaign group South Western Railway Watch (SWR Watch) meets The Telegraph outside Guildford Station, and immediately points out a limp, ripped National Rail flag outside.

“Look at the state of that,” he says. “Replacing it won’t make trains run on time but it symbolises the indifference; they haven’t even bothered to replace it.”

Recently, Varns pulled together the many complaints he hears from passengers into a 12-point letter to SWR management, categorising everything from dirty trains and unusable toilets to delays, broken information screens and failures of communication. What happened when he met the directors to work through some of these issues was revealing.

“They were kind of grilling me and asking whether I thought they were incompetent,” he laughs. “And I said, ‘No, I’m not necessarily saying you’re incompetent, but you’re clearly not delivering for your passengers – what you’re telling us is happening is completely different to what’s happening on the ground.’

“My biggest concern is that there’s still no published contract for members of the public to go and read what South Western is required to deliver,” he says. “That smacks of an obvious lack of transparency.

“It means there’s no consequences for failure. Yes, they have these big initiatives like drones being sent to investigate track problems. But when passengers get onto a train and none of the toilets are working, and it’s a bit grubby, and the information screens are not being repaired when they go wrong for several weeks… it gives this whole impression of, well, a railway that is a bit rubbish. Neglected.”

Which is not what nationalisation was supposed to deliver. Last month SWR published an “Improving Your Railway” plan to “make the short, medium and long-term changes that will deliver a railway you can rely on to get you where you need to be every day”.

It talks about how South Western will become part of Great British Railways next year, and focus on “fixing the fundamentals”.

Which is in line with Andy Burnham’s current attitude towards railway performance. He acknowledged during an interview in September that the entire rail network had “a difficult summer” and the situation wasn’t “good enough”. According to figures released by the Office for Rail and Road in September, punctuality improved for just three out of 25 operators between April and June this year, in comparison with the same period in 2025.

“I’ve lost count of the number of times someone has stopped me to tell me about the train that never came,” Prime Minister Andy Burnham admitted. When he was later asked by BBC South specifically when SWR would improve, he said: “It will get better… the railways are in need of repair and that will take some time. I realise passengers can’t wait forever, which is why I’m calling a rail summit for later this year.”

The problem is, those passengers waiting forever have little confidence, based on long experience, that any of these improvements will happen.

“Rail nationalisation is an ideology without an actual delivery plan behind it,” says Varns. “It’s meaningless in that sense, all of this is just people saying they understand that things aren’t very good and they will get better, when in fact it’s poor management and poor oversight at the heart of these problems.

“Ministers come and go, they’re looking for short-term fixes, when really what the railway infrastructure needs is a long-term plan, solving long-term funding.”

These are exactly the kind of concern Will Forster, the Liberal Democrat MP for Woking, hears all the time from his constituents. The Woking MP established an All Party Parliamentary Group to scrutinise SWR before nationalisation, and, he says, since then: “Things have got slowly, steadily worse… in fact it’s quite noticeable how bad things have got since it was nationalised.”

Forster has since launched his own constituency survey, and it revealed a service that is struggling to meet demand – particularly during the working week – alongside widespread frustration about unreliability and a continual lack of communication during disruption.

“In June I said in the Commons that nationalisation has not gone to plan. I wanted to know why and was told by the Leader of the House that we didn’t need a debate because things were expected to improve. But improve by what? There’s no measurement there, no KPIs, which is absolutely shocking.

“Now I’m not even sure there is a plan. At the moment it feels like this is being done by Labour because instinctively it will make them feel better as a party – which doesn’t seem to be helping.”

“I don’t expect next month all trains on SWR will run on time,” he adds. “But I do expect them to maintain performance, then improve it. This is not about Labour feeling better about themselves, this is about people arriving on time for work.”

Rail industry expert and author, Christian Wolmar, agrees with the need for a long-term plan, but thinks it is too early to write off nationalisation.

“South Western was a malfunctioning railway beforehand so you can’t expect it to turn around overnight. Actually, you can point to other franchises such as Southeastern which are back in public ownership where things have improved. Greater Anglia is doing very well.

“Ultimately improving railways is about structural change... the key question really is whether government allow – and create – a structure that allows the railways to be run by railway people.”

Forster says he will continue to press Government for answers and transparency, but when we put the questions and concerns that passengers tell us to the Department for Transport (DfT), the response comes with exactly the kind of unfettered optimism that infuriates the likes of SWR Watch’s Jeremy Varns.

While admitting there was “more to do” in a statement to The Telegraph, a DfT spokesman added: “South Western Railway passengers are seeing the benefits of public ownership, with 60 new 10-car Arterio trains now in service, increasing capacity across the London commuter network by more than a third and replacing a 40-year-old fleet with modern, more comfortable trains.

“This summer, traincrew-related cancellations were reduced by almost 84 per cent compared with last year, while the number of trains running with fewer carriages than planned fell by around 40 per cent.”

And if it seems like there is “more to do” is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that statement, then it’s the response of Lucy, returning home from a busy day’s work in London that sums up just how low confidence has become in South Western Railway since privatisation.

“For me, I hate travelling by train because of the poor service,” she says. “I try to use South Western just once a week now. It could be a lot better.”

data.title: Elon Musk invests $1bn in CNN-owner Skydance
data.description:
Elon Musk has pumped $1bn (£746bn) into the Hollywood giant Skydance, handing the billionaire a stake in the newly formed company behind CNN.

The Tesla founder was said to have made the commitment alongside new investment from other shareholders, including Laurene Powell Jobs, the widow of Steve Jobs, the founder of Apple, Semafor reported.

The cash injection will hand Mr Musk influence over Hollywood’s newest conglomerate, which was formed through the $110bn takeover of Warner Bros by Paramount earlier this month.

In addition to the major film studios behind Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, including HBO Max and Paramount+ streaming services, Skydance owns the CNN and CBS News networks.

The investment is significant because it will repay a favour to Larry Ellison, the Oracle tycoon who controls Skydance.

He provided $1bn in backing for Mr Musk’s takeover of Twitter in 2022.

John Malone, the cable tycoon behind Liberty Global, predicted the move earlier this week because of the close ties between Mr Musk and Mr Ellison.

“Who helped Elon finance Twitter when he bought it? Larry Ellison,” he told a conference on Wednesday.

“How did Larry Ellison come up with some of the money to put into the creation of Skydance? Tesla stock. And I would not doubt for a minute that before too long you’re gonna see an announcement.”

Mr Musk’s investment will help to shore up Skydance’s balance sheet after the debt-fuelled merger.

The company has a net debt of roughly $80bn, prompting concerns that its strategy will be governed by the need to lower its borrowing costs. Bosses have already said they will seek cost-savings of $6bn.

The move will also ease some of the pressure on Mr Ellison, who provided a $40bn personal backstop for the deal.

However, it may also trigger fresh concerns that the pair are teaming up to create a new Right-wing media empire in Hollywood.

Both billionaires are allies of Donald Trump, who this month said that Skydance would be a “great company”.

Paramount has already faced fierce scrutiny for its influence on CBS after a raft of changes at the broadcaster.

Mr Ellison and his son David have been accused by unions of editorial interference after a string of programming changes and cuts, including on its flagship news show 60 Minutes.

Christiane Amanpour, CNN’s long-serving chief international anchor, earlier this year criticised the “ideological realignment of CBS” and the “destruction, potentially” of 60 Minutes.

Mark Thompson, the former BBC director general who leads CNN, has insisted that Skydance “both understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for”.

Nevertheless, Mr Musk’s entry into the fray will raise fresh questions about the tycoon’s growing grip on the media.

Mr Musk’s $44bn takeover of Twitter has been beset with controversy and prompted a boycott by advertisers concerned about the spread of harmful material on the website.

Ofcom is currently investigating the social media app, now known as X, after it emerged its Grok chatbot was being used to undress women in photographs and generate child sexual abuse images.

Mr Musk’s investment in Skydance raises the prospect of content partnerships between Skydance and X, as well as potential tie-ups with SpaceX, which owns the satellite internet company Starlink.

Skydance was contacted for comment.

data.title: Parking fines capped at £100 in purge on ‘cowboys’
data.description:
Parking penalties are to be capped at £100 as Andy Burnham cracks down on so-called “cowboy” companies.

Motorists will also be given 10 minutes to leave car parks without facing a penalty once their paid-for time is up, under new legally binding rules due to come into force by the end of the year.

The Private Parking Code of Practice will give drivers the right to have charges cancelled on appeal for honest mistakes.

These include a breakdown in a car park, a medical emergency or a broken ticket machine, as well as stopping briefly to check directions and issues outside the driver’s control.

Mr Burnham said: “Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.

“These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them.

“We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes, while going after the deliberate scams that rip drivers off.”

Under the code, drivers who make mistakes such as forgetting parking permits, entering a vehicle registration wrong or forgetting to confirm it in a parking machine, will face a maximum charge of £20, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said.

At present, Westminster council, for example, issues penalties of up to £130. These increase to £195 for a single contravention if not paid within 14 days.

Simon Williams, the RAC’s head of policy, said the code was a “step in the right direction” to protect drivers from the practices of some private parking companies, but “not the leap” the motoring services company had been campaigning for.

He said: “We’ve long called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of parking charge notices and a single independent appeals body to replace the two industry-run ones, but neither have been included, which is disappointing.

“That said, the fact we finally have a code seven years on from the Private Parking Code of Practice Act becoming law is positive.”

A similar parking code of practice was issued in 2022 by the Conservative government. The parking industry robustly challenged it, prompting that set of rules to be withdrawn almost straight away.

Yet over-aggressive parking enforcement has been one of the nation’s biggest bugbears for many years.

In 2017, a Scottish woman was given a £24,500 penalty after ignoring more than 200 penalties, while in 2025 a nurse was taken to court by a private parking company after she “repeatedly” took more than five minutes after entering the car park to buy a ticket.

Will Hurley, the chief executive of the International Parking Community trade body, said: “I genuinely hope the new code is a good thing for the industry. We’ve put so much work into making sure that the Government understands the importance of it.

“For years I’ve been trying to change this mindset within the sector,” he added.

“Instead of looking for a reason to issue a charge, or instead of looking for a reason to reject an appeal [against a parking penalty], look for a reason not to issue a charge, or look for a reason to cancel a parking charge on appeal. And it’s just a slightly different mindset that I genuinely think makes a difference.”

A record 16.9 million parking tickets were handed out by private businesses in the 12 months to the end of March, according to analysis of government data by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation.

That is up from 14.4 million the year before, and 6.8 million in 2018-19. The parking industry attributed the rise to an increase in the number of car parks being managed.

Each ticket can be up to £100, meaning the total cost to drivers may be more than £4.6m per day at the current rate.

Alison Tooze, chief policy officer at the British Parking Association, said the new code was an “an important step forward for motorists, communities and responsible parking operators”.

“Overall, the code strikes the right balance between stronger protections for motorists and effective parking management, helping keep communities, businesses and local economies moving,” she said.

Jack Cousens, the head of roads policy at the AA, said: “After seven long years, drivers finally have something which could offer them better protections against the worst private parking operators. For too long, many private parking operators have aggressively attacked drivers to the point where many simply pay up if they receive a charge from one on the doorstep.

“While this is a good first step, there is still a huge amount of work to do, such as tackling the scourge of debt recovery fees. Ultimately, we need to stop charges being issued in the first place, especially where the driver has done nothing wrong.”

data.title: Clooney accused of hypocrisy in row with steel magnate
data.description:
George Clooney has been accused of hypocrisy in a court case being brought against a human rights organisation he co-founded.

A Libyan businessman has suggested that The Sentry, which investigates war crimes, failed to apply the standards that the US actor demands of news organisations that print stories about his private life.

Clooney, who is one half of The Sentry’s two-man advisory board, has in the past condemned British tabloids for “irresponsible” and “dangerous” journalism when they have written about his family, and has accused the media in general of failing to check their facts.

Ahmed Gadalla, a steel magnate, has instigated defamation proceedings against The Sentry after it published a 25-page report accusing him of money laundering, gun running and funding Russian mercenaries.

Mr Gadalla claims in court documents that the report’s “entire narrative was false” and that The Sentry “does not meet even the standard of a tabloid” because it failed to check its facts and refused to print Mr Gadalla’s response to its claims.

Legal papers filed in a court in Washington DC criticise Clooney, saying: “When the false story was about his own family, The Sentry’s co-founder applied a very different standard. In July 2014, after a British tabloid published such a story, George Clooney condemned the ‘irresponsibility’ of publishing it as ‘at the very least negligent and more appropriately dangerous’.”

A spokesman for The Sentry said: “Given the nature of our work, The Sentry is no stranger to efforts by powerful people who use litigation to silence critical speech that they dislike. We are reviewing the complaint and look forward to defending against any allegations.”

Actor rejects apology

Within two days the newspaper in question, the Daily Mail, removed the article and apologised, but Clooney refused to accept the apology.

He said at the time: “There is one constant when a person or company is caught doing something wrong. The cover-up is always worse.”

Clooney founded The Sentry with John Prendergast, a US human rights activist, in 2016, later merging it with Not on Our Watch, a humanitarian charity founded by Clooney, fellow actors Matt Damon, Brad Pitt and Don Cheadle, film producer Jerry Weintraub and lawyer David Pressman.

Clooney and Cheadle, who both starred in the film Ocean’s Eleven, make up the two-man advisory board of The Sentry. Clooney has reportedly donated $1m (£750,000) to The Sentry through his Clooney Foundation for Justice.

Clooney has repeatedly spoken about what he sees as a decline in media standards, saying that news stories used to require two reliable sources, but “that doesn’t seem to exist much any more”. His father Nick is a former journalist and news anchor.

According to the court documents filed by Mr Gadalla, in April The Sentry “falsely told the world that Mr Gadalla bankrolled a warlord’s assault on his own country’s capital with stolen public money, that he paid Russia’s Wagner Group mercenaries, that he secretly controls three Libyan banks and uses them to commit fraud and launder money, that he oversaw the printing of counterfeit currency in Russia and that he smuggles combat drones and military hardware in violation of a United Nations arms embargo”.

The Sentry called on the EU, the UN security council and four governments to impose sanctions on Mr Gadalla and on Libya’s prosecutors to charge him.

Mr Gadalla claims that the entire Sentry report was based on a wrongful claim that he had used a series of Emirati companies to borrow $300m from a bank in Abu Dhabi, secured by a guarantee of Libyan public money.

data.title: 130-year-old dog newspaper closes as Kennel Club plans rival
data.description:
The world’s oldest dog magazine has closed after the Royal Kennel Club unveiled plans to launch a rival publication.

Our Dogs, which was launched 130 years ago, said its new competitor and the “adverse financial climate” had forced it to shut down operations with the loss of 18 jobs.

The magazine was founded in 1895 by Theophilus Marples, a vicar’s son from Derbyshire, after he retired from judging dog shows.

A contemporary of Charles Cruft, whose eponymous dog show has been running for 135 years, Marples’ kennel included breeds ranging from Pomeranians and pugs to sporting spaniels.

The publication, which served an audience of pedigree dog breeders, handlers and show judges, went to press every week through world wars, epidemics and financial crises.

However, it has been battling a decline in advertising revenues as audiences shift online and has racked up losses of more than £1m in the last three years.

Our Dogs said the decision to end publication followed the Royal Kennel Club’s plans to launch a new publication next year.

The online outlet will combine the existing Kennel Gazette, which closed its print title last month, with its Journal and Field Trials newsletter.

Bosses also pointed to new regulations requiring judges’ critiques from dog shows to be sent to the Kennel Club site rather than Our Dogs, which they described as the “final nail in the coffin”.

A spokesman said: “The team have done our best to keep going with great features and special issues but there comes a point when, sadly, a decision has to be made.”

Scores of specialist magazines have been forced to close in recent years amid ballooning costs and dwindling advertising revenues.

The closure comes almost a decade after Our Dogs’ closest rival, Dog World, went into administration.

Kate Green, the deputy editor of Country Life magazine, said the launch of Our Dogs came amid a shifting attitude towards canines in Britain with Queen Victoria on the throne.

She said: “Queen Victoria changed our relationship with dogs. She changed the idea of keeping pets.

“Prior to her there were cur dogs, working dogs, and fighting dogs. Dogs became companions and much-loved pets and care generally improved.”

The magazine’s archive of around 7,000 issues is held in Manchester. Former executives plan to digitise the archive, allowing readers to access it globally.

data.title: NatWest forces thousands of remote workers back to the office
data.description:
NatWest is forcing tens of thousands of staff members back into the office in the latest crackdown on remote working.

The high street bank has told roughly 13,500 “remote-first” employees who currently go into work just two days a month that they will be expected in the office at least two days a week.

The new policy will also require a further 17,000 hybrid workers, who currently only have to be in the office for three days a fortnight, to come in more regularly. The changes will come into effect from February next year.

Exceptions will be allowed for those with caring responsibilities or medical issues, but will be determined on a case-by-case basis.

Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, said the policy change was “out of touch” and showed “contempt” for workers.

She said: “This is yet another kick in the teeth for workers who have suffered years of real-terms pay cuts and who are struggling to make ends meet.

“NatWest’s decision is completely out of touch with the realities facing its workforce. Thousands of workers face higher travel and childcare costs and disruption to caring responsibilities.”

NatWest is the latest in a string of major banks that have faced pushback from staff against attempts to mandate office attendance.

Barclays delayed an overhaul of its hybrid working policy last month, which would have compelled employees to work in the office three days a week.

The changes will now take effect at the start of 2027 after a backlash from staff, who demanded extra pay to cover commuting costs and exemptions for any employees whose commutes were longer than 40 minutes.

Meanwhile, staff at TSB have started preparing legal action to challenge plans to force them to work in the office three days a week following the bank’s £2.7bn takeover by Santander.

The Government has pledged to make it harder for employers to block staff from working remotely and has outlined plans to require businesses to “properly consider” flexible work requests.

The changes would require companies to hold a face-to-face meeting with staff to explain why their home-working requests had been rejected.

A NatWest spokesman said: “Flexible working remains an important part of how we work but we’ve also learned more about the value that spending time together brings for our colleagues and customers – helping teams collaborate, share ideas, build relationships and learn from one another.

“That’s why we’re introducing a more consistent approach across the bank, with colleagues expected to spend at least two days a week in the office, depending on the needs of their role and business area.”

data.title: Police froze shadow bank’s accounts amid fraud claims
data.description:
Police froze several bank accounts linked to a British shadow bank which collapsed amid claims of a £1.3bn fraud, it has been revealed.

The City of London Police, which polices the Square Mile, secured freezing orders against a number of bank accounts related to Market Financial Solutions (MFS).

Paresh Raja, the founder of MFS, allegedly received more than £400m from “funds managed by MFS” to “personal bank accounts” in the UK, Monaco, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates, according to a separate lawsuit.

Mr Raja has denied any wrongdoing and has consistently maintained that there was no fraud or dishonesty.

The frozen bank accounts belonged to a series of special-purpose companies that owned properties linked to MFS, according to filings by administrators.

However, the freezing orders were set aside in July. The administrators did not disclose why the orders were obtained or set aside, or whether any individual related to MFS was under investigation.

The City of London Police confirmed it was not investigating the collapse of MFS, and that the matter had been referred to the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

Some of MFS’s creditors have alleged that the properties were bought through nominee companies with money taken from MFS, held for the benefit of Mr Raja.

He is contesting these claims and has said the properties were held for the benefit of the business, not for himself.

Trust documents and consolidated company information related to MFS have also been passed on to the City of London Police.

Founded in 2006, MFS described itself as a specialist provider of buy-to-let mortgage lending and bridging finance. As a shadow bank, it funded its loans by borrowing from banks and other lenders.

Its creditors include a cast of important names in the City and Wall Street, including Barclays, Santander, Wells Fargo and Jefferies.

The company’s demise has shocked the City and spurred a number of investigations. Allegations of fraud following its insolvency have further stoked concerns around lax underwriting standards in the booming asset-backed lending markets.

The Financial Reporting Council, which regulates auditors, has opened an investigation into three small accountancy firms that worked for MFS.

The FCA has also opened an enforcement investigation into the stricken mortgage lender.

Officials from the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) have also requested information from lenders, including Barclays, that backed MFS.

The PRA, a division of the Bank of England that regulates lenders, is reportedly concerned about insufficient risk assessment and due diligence by banks on MFS and its related companies, according to the Financial Times.

The banking watchdog is also investigating whether banks have indirect exposure through lending to private capital groups that may have backed MFS independently.

Representatives for Mr Raja declined to comment.

data.title: Burnham has backed himself into a corner over public control of Thames Water
data.description:
The quest to save Thames Water is the saga with no end. Two and a half years after shareholders abandoned the company, its future is no more certain.

On the contrary, it is even more of a financial basket-case now than it was then, having been kept afloat by a steady drip-feed of emergency loans at a business that was already drowning in debt.

Additional borrowings since March 2024 stand at roughly £3bn with another £2.4bn on the cards, just to see it through the next 12 months.

That assumes, of course, that a disparate creditor base can agree on a deal – far from a foregone conclusion despite the high stakes.

The arrival of Andy Burnham in No 10 would bring an end to this financial purgatory, we were told.

Under Showtime Andy a privately led, debt-heavy industry ownership model that prioritised shareholder enrichment rather than customer care would be consigned to the dustbin, replaced by a system of greater “public control” – even though no one in Government has been able to explain what that means.

Burnham’s intervention has been characteristically cack-handed. Instead of steadying the ship, the Prime Minister has done precisely the opposite, exacerbating the uncertainty.

The problem is his propensity to speak first without thinking about the consequences. Just three months into his Premiership, a clear pattern has already been established: Burnham’s desire to be popular means he cannot help but put his foot in his mouth.

On Thames Water, he has backed himself into the tightest of corners. Burnham’s enthusiasm for nationalisation was such that it was widely assumed it would be among the first truly meaningful things the former mayor of Manchester would do upon setting foot in Downing Street.

The problem is that nobody in government, including the Prime Minister, paused to consider whether such a move was even plausible. Everyone was too concerned with playing to the gallery, telling an exasperated British public what it was assumed it wanted to hear.

But as ministers have quickly discovered, there is a big difference between wanting to do something and being able to, and the reality is that he inherited a country that cannot afford public ownership of critical assets such as Thames.

Some Labour figures have allowed themselves to be fooled into thinking that the Government could simply seize control without having to buy out the creditors.

But as has been pointed out, including in this column, such a move would amount to expropriation, something more associated with failing Communist regimes.

It’s fine to talk about wanting to end neoliberalism, but the reality is that the UK economy is massively reliant on foreign capital, much of it from long-term investors of the sort that had been lending to Thames long before the Wall Street hedge funds turned up.

Government contempt for the rule of law and property rights would be devastating to this country’s standing.

But even if Thames could be nationalised without recourse to the creditors, there is another glaring flaw that the pro-nationalisation crowd are unable to address: where will the investment come from afterwards?

There can be no doubt that water suppliers and their many shareholders are guilty of woeful underinvestment in the industry stretching back many years, something that a supine regulator must take some of the responsibility for.

But the country’s decrepit Victorian pipes and filthy waterways require a staggering £290bn of funding in the next 25 years just to ensure the taps stay on and our rivers are cleaned up.

These are figures from the National Audit Office, which also points out that at the current rate, it would take 700 years to renew the entire network.

Does this Government have that sort of money lying around? Of course not – not even close. It’s preposterous to even suggest that nationalisation of the water sector, or even just Thames, is somehow feasible.

Yet having seen his rhetoric collide with reality, the Prime Minister refuses to accept defeat. Officials are being told to come up with other ideas that would enable him to claim his promise of greater public control has been achieved.

The latest half-cocked plan supposedly on the table is to convert £100m of fines into a government stake, but a fag-packet calculation suggests that would equate to around 3pc of the company.

Not only is that close to meaningless, the creditors would still own the vast majority of it – something Labour MPs have made it clear they are vehemently opposed to.

It would also mean letting the company off a slew of fines for pollution when ministers have made a big song and dance about ensuring irresponsible water suppliers are properly held to account for any damage to the environment.

The result is a dangerous stalemate that will come back to bite the Prime Minister.

Burnham refuses to give his blessing to a restructuring proposal that’s been on the table for 18 months and will result in billions of pounds of Thames Water’s debts written off along with billions more in fresh equity pumped into the business.

Yet he and his team are yet to come up with any credible alternatives.

If the hedge funds aren’t the answer, and the Government doesn’t have a plan B, then what instead?

Wouldn’t a better solution be one in which the private sector continues to provide the vast financial resources required but under a regime of greater outside oversight and governance?

This can be done without the need for full nationalisation or for the state to have any economic interest at all.

Thames Water’s creditors have already agreed to a dividend freeze. They are willing to give the Government a golden share too, and the idea of allowing local mayors to have representation on its board has been floated too.

There could be an employee representative as well, which is the model in many European countries. Perhaps the privately held suppliers could also be partially floated on the stock exchange, a move that would guarantee much greater transparency and scrutiny.

There are many versions of this, but the Government urgently needs to clarify what its position is.

The longer Thames is left in limbo, the greater the risk that the vilified investors who have been propping it up will lose patience and walk away, leaving the Government to attempt to contain the fallout. This includes ensuring services aren’t interrupted.

If that happens, ministers will be responsible for one of the most spectacular slow-motion car crashes of all time.

data.title: Germany’s top banker sounds alarm over French debt crisis
data.description:
Germany’s most senior banker has sounded the alarm on France’s debt crisis after nationwide riots raised fresh concern about the country’s public finances.

Christian Sewing, the chief executive of Deutsche Bank, said the situation evolving in France was “concerning” as recent clashes caused fresh instability in financial markets.

His comments came as the cost of government borrowing in France surged to its highest level in 24 years.

The yield on 10-year French bonds – the effective interest rate it pays to borrow money – climbed above 5pc for the first time since 2002 on Wednesday.

Mr Sewing, who heads Germany’s flagship bank, called for a “disciplined budget” to bring France’s deficit back under control.

“The bond market is not lying,” he said.

Investors signalled their concerns about the state of France’s public finances on Wednesday as the divide between the borrowing costs of Europe’s two largest economies widened to its biggest gap in 15 years.

“The situation in France is obviously concerning and will remain volatile, I think, up to the elections in May,” Mr Sewing told Bloomberg TV.

“I wouldn’t call it a debt crisis at this point in time, but I think it’s a wake up call in particular for all public financing that budget disciplinary is key.”

He added: “It is so important, in particular in times like we live, you have a disciplined budget, you have your debt under control.”

France’s debt costs have climbed amid concern that recent unrest is an indication that its government will not be able to win enough support to stabilise the nation’s finances.

More than half a million people took to the streets in France at the weekend in the largest demonstrations since the pension reform strikes of 2019 and 2023, and the “yellow vests” movement of 2018.

However, the protests against school underfunding and the cost of living descended into looting and violence, with more than 2,300 people arrested.

Carrefour, the French supermarket giant, saw its shares plunge more than 14pc on Wednesday after it cut its full-year profit targets as a result of damage caused by the protests.

Alexandre Bompard, the supermarket’s chief executive, said on Monday that the chain faces a €10m (£8.4m) repair bill as a result of the unrest.

The company warned in its third-quarter results: “In light of the worsening social and security situation, the group considers that consumption trends and operating conditions in France are facing a deterioration.”

Alexandre Stott, an economist at Goldman Sachs, said the violence was hurting French markets.

He said: “The possibility of further disruptions poses an additional risk to an economy already weakened by tighter financial conditions, elevated political uncertainty and contractionary fiscal policy.”

In contrast to France, the UK’s cost of borrowing fell on Wednesday amid expectations that the Budget will not lead to sharp rises in taxes or spending. The yield on 10-year gilts, as UK bonds are known, fell from 5.41pc to a 5.35pc.

France’s parliament votes next month on whether to approve the budget for 2027 put forward by Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, which aims to rein in public spending.

However, populist candidates for next year’s presidential election have promised to continue spending.

Both Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who are gaining in the polls, have pledged to bring the country’s retirement age down from 64 to 62.

Concerns about France’s public finances have also hurt the euro, which has slumped by more than 1pc against the pound in the last week to be worth 83.8p.

Peter Kinsella, the head of UK investment services at Swiss private bank UBP, said: “The European Central Bank cannot credibly intervene in the absence of a French cost cutting programme, and that will not happen until after the presidential election next May.

“So, this is going to be a thorn in the side of the euro for a while.”

data.title: American Express to axe 3,500 jobs
data.description:
American Express is poised to cut around 3,500 staff as the credit card company seeks to offset rising costs, raising the prospect of redundancies in the UK.

Steve Squeri, the company’s chief executive, said it would axe 5pc of its 78,000-strong workforce.

It remains unclear where the cuts will be made within American Express’s global workforce. The company has 1,500 employees based in its London office.

Mr Squeri said that the job cuts were part of an effort to make American Express more efficient and speed up decision making across the business.

American Express posted third-quarter earnings which beat estimates, with Mr Squeri saying that the company’s “momentum continues”.

However, costs climbed about 9pc to $14.5bn (£10.9bn) in the third quarter. US bank regulators fined American Express $350m in October after the lender failed to identify potential money laundering ​activities worth billions of dollars.

Mr Squeri said American Express needed to become ​more “agile and efficient”.

Banks and other financial companies around the world have been shedding their job count in recent months as they look to streamline costs and continue to implement artificial intelligence across workflows.

Barclays announced this week that it would eliminate 5,000 jobs this year in one of the biggest tech-driven employment culls yet seen in the UK. HSBC and Citigroup are also cutting jobs.

Unite has accused Barclays of using AI as a smokescreen to push through redundancies, a charge the bank has denied.

Bill Winters, the boss of Standard Chartered, previously faced widespread criticism for referring to AI replacing “lower-value human capital”, as he announced 8,000 redundancies.

data.title: People who blare out music on public transport warned of £1,000 fines
data.description:
Passengers who play loud music on trains will be threatened with fines of up to £1,000 in a drive to stamp out anti-social behaviour.

Rail companies will target noisy commuters with announcements reminding them to put on headphones or face being thrown off at the next station.

Andy Burnham said that tackling inconsiderate travellers would help “make journeys that little bit better for all of us”.

The Prime Minister will front the launch of a government-backed campaign on Monday urging passengers to “share the carriage, not the noise”.

Train companies, including state-owned Great British Railways, will put notices across the network warning that playing music can be an offence.

Rail staff will be encouraged to first ask any traveller breaking the rules to put headphones in.

If they refuse to comply, they will be told they can be thrown off the train at the next station and face prosecution, with a maximum fine of £1,000.

Incidents where passengers refused to comply would initially be dealt with by train guards, with prosecutions brought by the British Transport Police.

Separate rules are also in place for buses, where loud passengers can be hit with on-the-spot fines of £100 by police for playing music aloud.

Drivers are not responsible for enforcing the rules, but are able to call in transport safety officers and the police to deal with incidents.

Mr Burnham said: “We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey.

“So, we’re launching a nationwide campaign reminding passengers to use headphones on trains. On top of that, we’re giving local leaders new powers to tackle loud music, vaping and littering on buses.

“It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.”

‘Share the carriage, not the noise’

Railway and bus companies are expected to promote the campaign on their services, as well as on their websites and across social media.

They will put up posters, and announcements have been recorded to play to passengers on trains.

One example provided by officials says: “This is a friendly reminder that you are in a shared space, so please consider those around you and wear headphones if you want to listen to music or take calls. Let’s share the carriage, not the noise.”

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, said: “It is so frustrating when the actions of an inconsiderate few spoil journeys for the rest of us, whether that is vaping, littering or blasting music out loud. 

“Even small changes in behaviour can make a massive difference to people’s experience on public transport.

Union concerns

But unions expressed concerns about the plans, warning they risked adding to the “avalanche of escalating abuse” that public transport workers faced.

Unite has demanded that bus drivers be given “the same protection from violence as emergency workers” when dealing with disruptive passengers.

Sharon Graham, the union’s general secretary, said: “The government’s proposals are well-meaning but wholly inadequate to tackle the challenges and violence bus workers are facing on a daily basis.

“The proposed penalties are not going to deal with the issues facing workers. Our members are demanding and deserve protections at work that these proposals do not address.”

data.title: Why even the Scots want BBC Scotland put out of its misery
data.description:
It was with a great deal of fanfare that the dedicated BBC Scotland TV channel was launched in 2019. After opening night, the corporation celebrated the fact that five of the top 10 most-watched programmes north of the border were on the station. Good news for fans of Still Game, a sitcom about two pensioners named Jack and Victor, and the sketch show Burnistoun Tunes In.

Some seven years (and a reported £200m) later, BBC Scotland is to be taken off air as new director-general Matt Brittin seeks to cut £500m from budgets by 2028. That first night was a high-water mark: viewing figures across the board quickly nosedived while The Nine, its flagship news programme, was an expensive failure and was scrapped not long after it emerged that one episode was watched by fewer than 2,000 people.

The drama and entertainment offering either fell flat or should have been on the nationwide channels from the get-go. For instance, Guilt, a drama starring Mark Bonnar, was good enough to be broadcast across the UK on BBC Two. On the other hand, how big a market is there for a chat show hosted by 2003 Pop Idol winner Michelle McManus?

However, like BBC Three, it will live on zombie-like as an online-only offering on iPlayer. Some shows commissioned by the channel will also be available on BBC One and Two, while the latter will carry more Scotland-only programming when the changes take effect in the spring. Reporting Scotland: News at Seven, which replaced The Nine in an earlier time slot, is to be entirely cancelled.

Dorothy Byrne, the former head of Channel 4 News, who is Scottish, laments the fact that the channel so obviously did not work. “Normally I might be one of those people who go, ‘I am Scottish, this is a tragedy for Scotland.’ I think it’s very sad, and I think it had some good things on it, but it never captured the imagination and attention of Scottish people in the way that it needed to.”

That may, at least in part, be a result of how BBC Scotland came into being. During and after the Scottish independence referendum campaign, the SNP government at Holyrood accused the BBC of being institutionally biased against self-determination for Scotland and failing to cater for licence-fee payers in the nation. Its launch was welcomed by Nicola Sturgeon, the First Minister at the time, when it was announced in 2017, and its demise has been called “unacceptable” by Màiri McAllan, the Scottish culture secretary.

Actual viewers seemed less bothered about whether the BBC Scotland brand lives or dies. “I sort of think if it hasn’t worked, just put it out of its misery,” Byrne adds. “Sometimes in Scotland, programmes are kept for fear of Scottish politicians, and that’s not how television should be made. The fact is, if the audience doesn’t want it… the audience are the people we should care about, not the politicians.”

At a time when the BBC needs to “make every pound work harder for audiences”, as Brittin said when the changes were unveiled, the sums did not add up in the channel’s favour. Just 12 per cent of the Scottish population use BBC Scotland each week, according to the corporation’s most recent annual report. (It is notable that BBC Alba, the Gaelic-language channel, reached 43 per cent of Gaelic viewers last year, after it bought the rights to broadcast Italian Serie A football.)

In 2024-25, BBC Scotland had a £42m budget that did not prove to be good value-for-money. Its “cost per user hour” – a measure of how much money it takes to get people to tune in – was 13p, which grew to 45p for viewing only on the BBC Scotland channel and its content on iPlayer. That compares unfavourably with BBC One (10p), BBC Two (9p) and BBC Four (6p).

The BBC has stopped including the cost-per-user-hour figure in its annual reports, beginning with the one published this summer. A cynic might suggest that is a way for the corporation to avoid embarrassing comparisons between its services. That is disputed inside the BBC. “It’s less about the channels and more about viewing, listening and browsing,” says an insider. “Content now goes farther than just a channel or service.” Regardless, BBC Scotland still has to save £10m, and the news about the channel’s closure will be accompanied by the loss of 10 jobs on top of 60 that were previously announced.

Those in the industry reckon it was inevitably going to be a challenge to make a BBC Scotland broadcast channel work at a time when it was obvious to most that viewers increasingly wanted to watch what they wanted, when they wanted, how they wanted. “It was always an odd decision to launch a new linear channel when viewing was already moving to on demand,” says Stewart Purvis, a veteran broadcasting executive. “There is undoubtedly a demand for more content about Scotland, and the money was and is best spent on producing programmes that can be accessed at any time.”

There will be changes needed for the new online-only offering to avoid going the way of its broadcast forebear. “Surely the BBC should be offering a one-click connection to all their content about Scotland,” says Purvis. “It’s one of the many oddities about iPlayer that maybe the director-general will sort out.”

data.title: Healey will deliver his Budget in dire economic circumstances
data.description:
John Healey is expected to do his best next week to deliver a Budget that various economists hope will “do no harm”.

That might sound welcome after years of heavy tax rises under his predecessor, Rachel Reeves.

Yet this is not an economy in which little is happening: steadying a sinking ship requires more than paralysis from the captain.

John Healey is presenting his maiden Budget in the worst of circumstances. Beset by spiralling borrowing costs, mounting debt – which passed the £3tn mark in September – and rising inflation, the Chancellor faces bad news wherever he looks.

Investment for the future looks weak, too: Liam Byrne, the senior Labour MP, warns “ministers have yet to grip the scale” of the challenge.

Despite heroic efforts to talk up the summer’s GDP growth numbers, the fact remains that growth slowed in August and more pain is on the way.

Price rise pain

Inflation shows the direction of travel: Consumer prices in September were up 3.5pc on the year, the steepest rise so far in 2026.

And it’s not just higher petrol and diesel prices driving up inflation any more. From building materials and carpets to telecoms and insurance, inflation is creeping up across more of the economy as higher fuel prices are passed on.

Food prices have not surged yet, but are expected to: a combination of taxes on retail, fertiliser shortages caused by the war in Iran, El Niño weather patterns and the higher cost of energy in production and distribution are all set to push up the bill for the weekly shop.

The hammer blow comes this winter. Ofgem’s energy price cap is poised to rise by almost a quarter in January, according to the Bank of England. Such a jump would take the typical home’s annual bill back above £2,000 for the first time since 2023.

That is not the only cost facing families. Mortgage rates are rising steeply and the Bank of England is expected to raise its base rate to 4pc at a policy meeting the week after the Budget.

More expensive essentials and bigger loan repayments suck household spending power out of the rest of the economy. This slows growth and undermines tax receipts. Paralysis in the housing market is particularly painful for a Government counting on stamp duty to bring in £20bn per year.

Into these agonies steps the Chancellor.

Healey is hemmed in by the borrowing rules, Labour’s own tax promises and the PM’s attempts to sprinkle good cheer on the populace with help for pubs here and a cut to VAT on electricity bills there.

Yet even a modestly sized Budget risks doing significant harm to the economy.

Bank tax fears

The biggest touted measure is a £2bn raid on banks, as Left-wingers view the industry as unreasonably profitable at a time of economic strife.

Healey plans to ramp up the corporation surcharge levied on their profits from 3pc to 8pc. The policy was initially introduced in the wake of the financial crisis to stop banks benefitting from any cuts to business taxes.

Now, the souped-up surcharge leaves lenders facing the highest corporation tax seen in Britain for 30 years.

This threatens to make all of the economic problems facing the country worse: a bank tax would push up mortgage rates, affecting inflation; it would hamper growth as banks pull back on lending; and it would probably make the national debt worse because welfare payments would rise with higher inflation.

The CBI warns attacking banks will hurt growth across the country. Andy Haldane, a former chief economist of the Bank of England and briefly a Burnham adviser, says it would “repel” investors.

That in turn would hit growth, prosperity, and, ultimately, the public finances that the tax is supposed to support.

A £2bn levy on the banks might seem like small fry in the broader context of the UK economy, but even minute changes in taxes can send outsized signals about a Government’s priorities.

Recall the 2012 Budget. Overall, George Osborne changed almost nothing. Tax decisions were forecast to reduce government revenues by £30m per year – yes, million, not the £25bn of the National Insurance raid of 2024 – and increase spending by £1.1bn.

Yet arguments over pasties and grannies meant it was rapidly branded the “omnishambles Budget”. Chaos and indecision reigned.

This time around, making banks the centrepiece will show a deep hostility to businesses. As Healey courts unions and praises the importance of their relationship with the Government, the private sector feels shunned and ripped off.

Any real interest in growth has evaporated, say those who have endured pre-Budget meetings with senior ministers.

Neither the PM’s “good growth in every postcode” nor “hope in every heart” will be found in the famous red despatch box next week.

data.title: The West is hooked on Chinese drugs but they could save your life
data.description:
Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to invite Sir Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca’s chief executive, to Beijing at the beginning of the year was a textbook piece of modern diplomacy.

The then-prime minister’s attempt to revive economic cooperation rested on a knockout deal that went beyond the usual warm words. Sir Pascal, a sworn Sinophile and one of the biggest cheerleaders of Chinese innovation, was only too happy to oblige.

Within hours of Sir Keir’s arrival, AstraZeneca had unveiled a plan to invest $15bn (£11bn) in China, building on its existing medical manufacturing and research capabilities in Beijing, Shanghai, Wuxi, Taizhou and Qingdao.

AstraZeneca’s pledge was the marquee announcement of Sir Keir’s trip. Sir Pascal said the “landmark investment” marked the next chapter for the company in China. For the politburo, it was further proof that their plan to turn China into a global pharmaceuticals leader has worked.

In the West, China has long been dismissed as little more than a dealer in cheap copycat medicines – both legal and illegal – and increasingly knockoffs too, such as unlicensed GLP-1 weight loss medication.

This portrayal no longer bears scrutiny, however. In recent years, the Chinese pharmaceutical industry has undergone a remarkable reinvention. Western industry leaders view it as a bona fide drug superpower at the forefront of discovery.

China controls an exciting pipeline of groundbreaking medicines and occupies a growing role as a globally important venue for clinical trials.

But for now, cooperation between East and West suits both sides. European and American drugmakers have rushed to embrace Chinese research, forging multi-billion licensing deals. Those with the appetite have opened their own labs and even set up manufacturing outposts.

Chinese science is now “the best in the world” and ignoring it is not an option, says one European pharmaceuticals chairman.

Few have led the charge as enthusiastically as Sir Pascal, AstraZeneca’s swashbuckling French boss. China is now its second-biggest market. Meanwhile GSK, the UK’s other national drug champion, has struck a series of partnerships with Chinese labs to licence promising drugs outside the country.

These relationships are critical for China’s pharmaceuticals industry, providing access to the lucrative markets that fund innovation. At home, their only customer is Xi Jinping, and he sets the price.

Yet this partnership is fragile. Amid growing concern in the US about the threat China’s new scientific prowess poses to drug supplies, innovation and even national security, industry executives fear an iron curtain will be drawn.

Drugs may be the next front in the superpower trade war that has already drawn in telecoms equipment, semiconductors, electric vehicles, rare earth minerals and solar panels.

For Europe, including Britain’s pharmaceutical giants AstraZeneca and GSK, the looming nightmare is that an American administration will sooner or later use its economic muscle to effectively outlaw their cooperation with China.

One senior figure says the possibility of a sweeping American crackdown is “probably the one question that keeps me awake at night”.

China’s rapid scientific progress

Dr Zhao Hong, a renowned Chinese cancer specialist, shocked thousands of Communist Party delegates in March last year: a Guangzhou-based biotech firm had developed a cancer drug that had outperformed the world’s bestselling equivalent in clinical trials.

The work of China’s Akeso Biopharma, lung cancer drug ivonescimab had shown that it could delay non-small-cell lung cancer progression for five months longer than US giant Merck’s Keytruda treatment – the world’s bestselling prescription drug in 2025.

The success of ivonescimab was hailed as a breakthrough moment for China’s pharmaceutical industry.

“China is at the best time of its biopharmaceutical sector’s development,” Hong told state media at the annual Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.

The speed with which China is catching up in pharmaceuticals and biotech is astonishing.

By 2024, China had 1,255 drugs at the research stage, a nearly eight-fold jump in less than a decade. America had 1,441 – a 15pc rise – while the total in Europe had shrunk slightly to 400.

Experts attribute the leap to a fundamental shift in how the industry was perceived by the Chinese regime.

One veteran UK executive recalls how when he first used to visit China in the late 1990s, it was to complain about “counterfeits and pharmaceuticals that were really dangerous”. Today, China is seen as “a golden opportunity”, he says.

“They have moved deliberately to be at the leading edge of science,” he adds.

Beijing has provided vast support in the form of scores of state-financed biotechnology parks equipped with advanced laboratories and heavily subsidised hardware, together with a sweeping overhaul of the regulatory system beginning in 2015.

A study by Prof Yimin Cui, of Peking University, and colleagues found that the time taken to approve a drug for human trials fell to 87 days after the reforms, from 501 days previously.

Chinese researchers are helped by the sheer size of the country’s population – last counted at more than 1.4 billion – says Freddy Yip, a corporate lawyer at Cooley.

“In the US, it may take a long time to recruit sufficient patients, but in China, you have access to lots of different patients with different kinds of diseases, including many rare diseases,” Yip says.

Sir Pascal has said this combination of scientific capability and rapid execution – “China speed”, as he has called it – can help to dramatically accelerate drug development.

One of China’s leading biotech venture capitalists estimates clinical trials are “two thirds cheaper and half as quick in China”.

Progress has been spurred by a massive increase in spending on research and development – leaping from $35m in 2015 to $15bn in 2023 – and a “reverse brain drain” in which thousands of foreign-educated Chinese scientists and entrepreneurs have returned home, according to Porsche Consulting.

Chinese scientists are now at the vanguard of treatment for cardiovascular diseases and cancer, as well as spearheading drug development for metabolic conditions and neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s, among many others.

Alarm bells in Washington

Mere months before Sir Pascal was lending heft to Sir Keir’s Beijing bridge-building mission, the Frenchman was being warmly welcomed at the Oval Office by Donald Trump.

Thanking the US president for welcoming him “in this beautiful office”, Sir Pascal was armed with another crowd-pleasing announcement: a pledge to cut drug prescription prices in the US, after Trump had accused other countries of “freeloading” at the expense of Americans.

Sir Pascal went further as well, unveiling a $50bn plan to expand the company’s existing operations in the US. In return, AstraZeneca received a three-year exemption from tariffs.

Privately, AstraZeneca executives acknowledge it was also an attempt to ward off growing concern in the White House about the deepening of ties with China.

“We are cognisant of some of the more hawkish commentary [from US politicians]. It is a delicate balancing act, and we are treading a fine line by recognising what the US is trying to achieve,” an insider says.

Yet, for all Washington’s alarm, dependency has become more pronounced, not less. Western companies have piled into the country, hoovering up clinical trial data and striking licensing deals to develop Chinese medicines outside the mainland, which they hope can then be used to treat patients across the developed world.

“This is the golden age of science and China is white-hot right now,” an industry source says.

Deal activity is being driven by anxiety among European and US companies as their pipeline of drugs peters out.

America’s biotech industry faces the alarming prospect of an estimated $350bn worth of medicines – equivalent to roughly one fifth of projected global prescription-drug revenue – losing patent protection by the end of the decade.

When patents run out, generic rivals are allowed to gatecrash the market, jeopardising sales.

Few have led the way with the verve that AstraZeneca has demonstrated.

Sir Pascal’s Beijing announcement was accompanied by a boast that it had signed 16 global licensing agreements with 15 Chinese partners since 2023 alone – thought to be the most of any overseas pharmaceuticals multi-national.

GSK hasn’t been far behind. Last year, the company struck an alliance with local giant Hengrui Pharma to develop a dozen new medicines outside the mainland. The value of the deal could eventually total $12bn.

The agreements are part of an industry-wide surge in deals totalling $138bn last year – a nearly tenfold jump since 2021 – according to data provider PharmCube. 2026 is expected to be another record.

Deal flow shows little sign of slowing.

A fortnight ago, GSK unveiled a $1.3bn pact with Hutchmed, a Hong Kong-based biopharmaceuticals company with research facilities in Shanghai, for the bulk of the licensing rights to what it called “first in-class” cancer treatments.

Brewing geopolitical storm

Amid the feeding frenzy, concern in Washington has turned to outright hostility in some quarters.

In December last year, Trump signed into law the Biosecure Act, a move widely seen as a sharp escalation in tensions and the moment the longstanding strategic rivalry between the US and China spilt into the biotechnology arena.

The act prevents US companies reliant on federal contracts and funding from working with Chinese biotech firms with ties to the Chinese military and any deemed to pose a national security risk. It also bars Chinese companies from accessing US government funding themselves.

US biotechnology companies with federal contracts are now engaged in a mad dash to purge their supply chains of equipment obtained from any Chinese biotechnology firms on the banned list.

Next up is the Biotech Investment National Security Act. Though not yet signed into law, it will subject licensing deals involving Chinese companies to national security reviews.

Though technically a screening mechanism rather than a ban on licensing Chinese drugs, it will effectively function as one, says Craig Garthwaite, a professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

There is also pressure to bar the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from accepting Chinese trial data, amid concerns about their reliability. The FDA has repeatedly rejected one of Hengrui’s cancer drugs, citing questions about quality control at its manufacturing sites.

As one senior City figure puts it: the White House has conjured up other reasons to “erect a wall around China”.

AstraZeneca’s attempt to navigate this geopolitical storm by investing in both China and the US divides opinion. Some see it as an inspired way to keep both Washington and Beijing happy at the same time.

“I think Pascal has been very smart in not allowing anybody to question his US credentials. He’s playing his cards very wisely,” the boss of a rival company says.

Others see it as a high-stakes gamble from a company that is more exposed than most of its competitors and has learnt the hard way the risks that come from operating in China.

Leon Wang, the former head of its Chinese operations, is awaiting trial on charges of illegal trading, unlawful collection of personal information and medical insurance fraud, alongside another former employee, having been arrested in 2024.

If the saga made Sir Pascal reconsider his appetite for doing business in China, there is little sign of it.

Alongside licensing deals potentially worth tens of billions of dollars, it has around 17,000 employees in China, two “global strategic” research and development centres in Beijing and Shanghai, and four advanced manufacturing sites in Wuxi, Taizhou, Qingdao and Beijing.

China is now AstraZeneca’s second-largest market after the US, accounting for roughly 12pc of the company’s global turnover, and its Chinese facilities supply more than 70 markets worldwide.

In a written submission to the Commons business and trade select committee in July, AstraZeneca described co-operation with China as a “win-win”.

But as one investor with extensive interests in China points out: “If you’re a big pharma company with a significant proportion of your licensing spend coming from China and the tap suddenly gets turned off, that’s obviously a problem.”

Europe’s wary response

Despite sharply rising tensions, there are concerns that European policymakers are still a long way off from having a coherent industrial strategy that addresses the China question.

Having been slow to react to the threat that cheap Chinese manufacturing poses to the continent’s steelmakers, solar panel producers and its car industry, the risk is that the pendulum swings too far the other way and Brussels takes a similarly antagonistic approach in trying to shut China out of other sectors, such as pharmaceuticals.

Calls by Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, for tougher trade measures against Beijing have been interpreted in some circles as a signal that EU-China relations are close to a tipping point after years of resistance to anti-Chinese duties from the continent’s car giants.

Yet, a senior industrialist says Europe lacks the “economic counterweight to be able to exclude China”.

“I don’t necessarily think it’s good in the long term for the US to do so, but I think it’s very dangerous for Europe,” he adds.

“We need a more nuanced industrial strategy that seeks Chinese expertise and cost effectiveness, and to somehow bring some of the economic benefit of that into Europe,” he says.

Such sentiment echoes a growing willingness among car manufacturers to partner with Chinese counterparts amid an onslaught of imports. Nissan’s decision to share its Sunderland plant with Chery, one of China’s largest car exporters, is expected to be among the first of many similar tie-ups.

Some believe the growing divide between Washington and Beijing because of pharmaceuticals may even present an opportunity for Europe.

“I’m sure Europe would be more than happy to take Chinese-developed products that are sold to them at a lower price than what they might otherwise get from the United States,” Garthwaite says.

As Brussels bureaucrats try to agree on a co-ordinated approach, the rhetoric, particularly among some influential Republicans, continues to harden.

Chris Klomp, a top lieutenant of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, has likened the situation to “a war”.

Anxiety has been heightened by a so-called “hot mic” incident at a Beijing military parade late last year, in which Vladimir Putin and Xi were overheard discussing the possibility that humans could live to 150 years old, thanks to advances in biotechnology.

Some China hawks saw it as further evidence that the US risked falling behind in the global race for domination in advanced science.

The Council on Foreign Relations, an influential American think tank, has called for reliance on China’s biotech know-how to be treated as a strategic vulnerability akin to critical minerals.

“The US (and just about every other nation) faces a growing risk that China will deliberately withhold essential pharmaceutical inputs as a tool of economic or political coercion … as China has done with rare-earth critical minerals,” it warned in June.

The Atlantic Council, another US think tank with a history of shaping American foreign policy, points out that the US is reliant on China for three quarters of some imported drugs and as much as 99pc of some raw materials that are critical to the production of certain key medicines.

What’s more, China’s 2020 export control law and 2021 biosecurity law “grant broad authority to weaponise pharmaceutical exports”, it said recently.

‘All in or all out’

AstraZeneca declined to comment on its position, but there are signs it is more nervous than it is willing to acknowledge.

It emerged in August that the company had held detailed discussions with American rival Bristol Myers Squibb about a potential £300bn mega-merger.

In seeking to substantially deepen its US footprint, AstraZeneca may have concluded that the best chance it has of escaping any crackdown is if the company can demonstrate it is willing to take action to address Trump’s demands for the “reshoring” of pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Radical corporate restructuring plans have also been explored in China. AstraZeneca previously looked at the possibility of carving out its Chinese business into a separate legal entity and listing it on the Shanghai stock exchange. Though nothing came of those plans, they were seen as an attempt to insulate it from mounting geopolitical tensions.

GSK, meanwhile, sees no reason for such drastic action. Publicly, all a spokesman is willing to say is that it has “a longstanding presence in China, to make sure patients can access our medicines and vaccines”.

“China is also increasingly a source of cutting-edge biopharma innovation, and we have established several important collaborations for potential new treatments in oncology, respiratory, immunology and inflammation,” the spokesman adds.

However, like AstraZeneca, it too has fallen foul of Beijing after the company was engulfed in a bribery scandal in 2014.

GSK was found guilty of bribing Chinese doctors and hospitals to prescribe its medical products and was forced to pay a record $490m fine.

That ordeal prompted GSK bosses to take a much more cautious approach in which its activities were limited to strict licensing deals rather than the asset-heavy approach of others, such as AstraZeneca.

“It [GSK] went through a very difficult time in China. The experience damaged the company immeasurably in terms of its willingness to take risks,” a City source says.

By focusing on developing local collaborations, GSK believes it can still capitalise on the opportunities in China while being “less vulnerable” than rivals who are more “asset-exposed”, an insider explains.

Yet, the same person admits it ultimately boils down to one question: “Are they [China] helping us long-term or are they harming us? And I can’t answer that, which is why we can’t afford to be all in or all out.”

Industry figures hope common sense prevails between the two superpowers.

Garthwaite acknowledges deals that come with potential national security risk should be scrutinised, while attempts to reduce American over-dependence on Chinese antibiotics are also to be applauded.

However, he says the White House needs to distinguish between drug production and drug development, which “shouldn’t be too hard”.

Another investor says patients don’t really care where the drugs come from, “as long as they’re subjected to the same trials”.

In response to a recent US ban on imports of humanoid robots, China’s foreign ministry said: “Protectionism does not make the US more competitive … it will only hurt the interests of US companies and consumers.”﻿

Yet, nor is it in China’s interests to actively undermine American science. Chinese drugmakers simply cannot afford to be shut out of Western markets, particularly the US, experts say.

“China is really vulnerable too. It has to rely on its export machine because it doesn’t have sufficient levels of internal consumption,” one analyst says.

Ultimately, industry sources admit they are at the mercy of an unpredictable Trump administration whose appetite for trade wars shows little sign of waning.

As one boardroom veteran puts it: “It’s akin to walking a tightrope – we’ll continue trying to walk it and hope we stay on.”

data.title: Energy Secretary’s former employer doubts North Sea wealth fund
data.description:
A think tank once led by Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, has criticised her plans for a North Sea wealth fund, saying it would be ineffective.

The New Economics Foundation (NEF), which Ms Fahnbulleh led between 2017 and 2023, said the proposed Energy Wealth Fund would fail in its aims because tax revenue from oil and gas drilling was too small to fund net zero plans.

The new fund was announced by the Energy Secretary this week alongside her decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field, with future North Sea tax receipts going into the vehicle.

But Blai Avià-Novoa, an economist at the New Economics Foundation, said: “Redirecting a small and declining revenue base to the national wealth fund will not be enough to deliver the green investment that the UK so desperately needs.

“It’s important to remember that North Sea oil and gas revenues are declining at an accelerated rate. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) says that revenues in 2028-29 will be just £0.2bn, less than a tenth of what they were in 2023-24.”

A think tank veteran, Ms Fahnbulleh left the NEF in 2023, shortly before she was elected to Parliament as MP for Peckham in the last general election.

The Treasury is launching the Energy Wealth Fund, which will sit within the existing National Wealth Fund, with a £2bn injection.

It is unclear whether only a share or all North Sea tax receipts will be redirected into the fund, or whether John Healey, the Chancellor, could unveil a new surcharge on the sector.

Mr Healey said on Wednesday that if Britain had invested revenues from the North Sea since the 1980s, “we’d have a British sovereign wealth fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds”.

The figure is based on internal Treasury modelling, assuming North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested and left to grow at a similar rate to Norway’s $2.4tn (£1.8tn) sovereign wealth oil fund.

Britain’s decision to launch an Energy Wealth Fund long after North Sea revenues peaked is unlikely to yield any such results, sceptics have said.

Simon French, an economist at Panmure Liberum, said: “If the UK wants to start now then it shouldn’t be buying green energy assets but probably a global equity ETF, a global bond fund, and buy back some of that gold sold 25 years ago.”

Britain’s initiative will pour money into green energy projects, though the sums fall far short of what is needed.

The OBR has estimated that the Government needs to spend £257bn in 26 years up to 2050 to hit net zero.

Mr Avià-Novoa said: “To truly shift the dial, state investment vehicles like the National Wealth Fund will need to be able to borrow on the capital market, like they already can in other European countries.”
