data.title: Microsoft Word used to monitor blackout risk
data.description:
Grid bosses have been urged to upgrade their “embarrassing” computer systems after it emerged that staff were using Microsoft Word and Excel to monitor parts of Britain’s power supply.

An independent investigation found that staff used general Microsoft Office software in the control room at the National Energy System Operator (Neso) to produce key reports and manually track spare generating capacity.

This includes monitoring blackout risk and running calculations that inform decisions on whether to issue market warnings.

In an investigation report, Neso was urged to find a replacement amid concerns the approach meant decisions were not properly logged. Other critics have claimed the setup is “insecure”.

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said: “The fact that the organisation tasked with keeping the lights on in this country are using Excel spreadsheets and Microsoft Word to keep logs and ensure the stability of our grid is, quite frankly, embarrassing.

“Neso has so many questions to answer. The report published yesterday raised far more questions than it answered.

“We need to see fundamental change within Neso. Not just the culture, but how they operate and how they ensure the critical job of keeping our lights on in this country goes on.”

In an investigation into whistleblower complaints at Neso, law firm Eversheds Sutherland was tasked with determining whether poor record-keeping deliberately obscured blackout risks.

Lawyers ultimately found no evidence of this, but they raised concerns that control-room staff kept shift reports in Microsoft Word in a way that meant earlier versions were overwritten and lost when a new one was saved.

At the same time, they highlighted how “management and monitoring spreadsheets” on Microsoft Excel were used to “track [electricity] demand figures, [generation] margin positions and shift narrative”.

These included a spreadsheet to monitor the need for electricity margin notices (EMNs), which Neso issues when supplies are tight, as well as more serious high-risk of demand control (HRDR) notices, which can precede controlled blackouts.

Some documents were kept in a cloud-based system that let engineers easily check how documents evolved with time.

But investigating lawyers warned that management and shift-handover documents were typically stored on a “local drive”, meaning previous versions could not be accessed and were “susceptible to retrospective alteration”.

One witness also described the security around them as “not great”, while another said the spreadsheet was cumbersome and could discourage staff from updating it regularly.

‘Much bigger issues’

In its recommendations, Eversheds Sutherland urged Neso to “consider how to remediate version control gaps for electronic operational records, including the migration of operational documents to a platform with automatic version history”.

Kathryn Porter, an independent energy analyst, warned that using Word documents and Excel spreadsheets was “inherently insecure and not appropriate for use in mission-critical applications”.

She said: “These are not only administrative records, but they are also used in handovers between shifts, for calculating electricity margins and to assess whether thresholds for EMNs and HRDR warnings have been reached.

“This raises much bigger issues than document version control: why is a spreadsheet being used for operational calculations that can influence decisions about the security of Britain’s electricity system?

“Why are these functions not performed within properly designed and tested operational software, using approved models, controlled inputs, automated calculations and a complete audit trail of any adjustments?”

The report also revealed that Neso control-room staff still relied heavily on handwritten notes to log their decisions throughout the day.

Neso stressed on Tuesday that Microsoft Word and Excel were not used to instruct power stations or manage the grid directly.

It also refused to say whether their use would be phased out.

A spokesman added: “The independent investigation concluded that there was no evidence to substantiate any of the specific allegations made against Neso.

“It identified improvements to record-keeping and version control, which we are acting on, but it did not conclude that the use of spreadsheets makes Neso’s operational arrangements insecure.”

data.title: Lime riders joust as knights in London
data.description:
Lime bike riders have been filmed dressed as knights and duelling in London.

The company has said its bikes are “not for jousting” after videos circulated on social media showed hundreds of people gathered in London Fields, east London, to watch Saturday’s event.

Artist Jack Carden and actor Cameron Carnegie-Brown, known as Camtholomew, were filmed jousting whilst riding the green rentable e-bikes.

Dressed in chainmail, red and black cloaks and armour, including helmets, the pair ride towards one another, brandishing striped poles.

The assembled crowd can be heard chanting “joust, joust, joust” before one of the men strikes the other with a “lance”, causing them to fall from the bike.

A spokesman for Lime said on Monday: “We always love seeing Londoners come together and build a sense of community in unexpected ways.

“While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first.

“Lime bikes are designed for getting around the city, not for jousting.

“We discourage anyone from attempting similar events, to help keep riders and those around them safe.”

Posting on social media before the event, Mr Carden said the “free public joust” was “performance art”.

In a video from the event posted to both competitors’ social media accounts, a voiceover says: “I want to remind you all why we are here. 

“Not only does this mean some artistic violence but to come together and celebrate art, to remind ourselves that we’re all the same and that what we need right now in this world is a little bit more love.”

A video on Mr Carden’s Instagram account of the joust has been watched more than four million times.

data.title: GB News to launch ‘all-British’ radio station
data.description:
GB News is to launch an “all-British” music radio station as the media company seeks to expand beyond TV and steal audiences from the BBC.

The new 24-hour digital station, named GB Music Radio, is slated to hit the airwaves next month with a playlist dedicated exclusively to artists from the UK.

The station will showcase six decades of domestic talent and play six hours of ad-free music on Saturdays in what it calls Great British Party Night.

GB Music Radio will also broadcast news bulletins on the hour, alongside traffic and travel updates.

One insider said the station was aiming to win market share from BBC Radio 2, claiming there was a “big opportunity” to poach listeners from the BBC.

Radio 2 has been battling a decline in ratings in recent years, with audience numbers for its breakfast show falling to a record low under Scott Mills.

The flagship show is now fronted by Sara Cox, who took over from Mr Mills after it emerged this year that he had been the subject of historical allegations of “serious sexual offences”.

Several “golden oldie” stations, including Boom Radio and Greatest Hits Radio, have grown in popularity as disenchanted listeners defect from Radio 2.

The launch of GB Music Radio will be spearheaded by GB Media, a new arm of the broadcaster aimed at expanding into new areas. Further new ventures are expected to be unveiled in the coming months.

It comes as GB News braces for the launch of Reform TV, a new online venture that threatens to splinter Right-wing audiences.

The party has built a new studio in Westminster and is hiring journalists for a national newsroom, while the launch has triggered fears that Nigel Farage, GB News’s biggest star, could defect.

GB News insiders have played down concerns about the new outlet, arguing that the broadcaster is not reliant on one presenter or political party.

Nevertheless, the channel is now seeking to broaden its appeal with programming that celebrates Britain’s cultural contributions.

The new radio station will also open up new opportunities for advertising as the company reels from a brand boycott led by the pressure group Stop Funding Hate.

GB News, which is owned by hedge fund tycoon Sir Paul Marshall and Dubai investment firm Legatum, cut around a third of its workforce over the summer in an effort to balance the books.

It has racked up losses of more than £140m since its launch in 2021.

GB News presenters Paul Coyte and Nana Akua will take up presenting roles on GB Music Radio for the weekday and weekend breakfast shows respectively. Both will continue in their existing roles on the news channel.

Liverpool-based broadcaster Rick Houghton will present the drivetime show.

A spokesman for GB Media said: “We are a media company that has demonstrated its commitment to celebrating Britain and its rich culture.

“The launch of GB Music Radio marks the first step in a series of initiatives designed to bring compelling and engaging content to more people across the nation.”

Ross Sergeant, the chief revenue officer at GB News, said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.

“British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners’ day, from Breakfast with Paul to weekend mornings with Nana.”

data.title: ‘Del Boy billionaire’ enters race for Poundland
data.description:
A British businessman nicknamed the “Del Boy billionaire” has joined the race to acquire struggling Poundland.

Chris Dawson, the 74-year-old Plymouth-born entrepreneur, is understood to be looking to purchase a selection of the discount retailer’s stores, according to The Times.

The founder of CDS Superstores, which owns The Range, Wilko and Homebase, is among a raft of suitors expressing interest in the budget retailer, which has been put up for sale by owner Gordon Brothers.

The US-based investment company acquired Poundland for £1 last summer as the retailer faced rising operational costs, fierce competition, and a consumer shift toward online shopping.

However, the decision to put it up for sale so soon after the takeover has raised fears that Poundland could be broken up or tipped into administration, putting jobs at risk.

Union officials at Usdaw, who are understood to have been offered a meeting with Poundland management, fear that owner Gordon Brothers may favour selling the business piecemeal.

Poundland has stressed its preference to sell the chain to Irish firm Martin Property Group, which holds real-estate interests spanning shopping centres to hotels.

Although no formal management buyout has been launched, Martin Property Group is backing interest led by Barry Williams, Poundland’s chief executive, and Andy Bond, its director. The firm is proposing a solvent acquisition and working with the board on a potential deal. It could be finalised as soon as this week.

However, bidders continue to circle in case talks falter.

Mr Dawson gained the nickname the “Del Boy billionaire” in the press as a reference to his yellow Lamborghini Urus, which has a personalised number plate “DE11 BOY”, a homage to the character Del Boy Trotter from Only Fools and Horses.

Like Del Boy, the businessman started his career as a market trader, before founding The Range and scaling it to a UK high street giant. He has since purchased both Wilko and Homebase out of administration.

A CDS spokesman said: “We don’t comment on market speculation. Our focus remains on growing our family of brands and delivering outstanding value for customers.”

Poundland has also attracted interest from turnaround firm Modella Capital, which owns WH Smith’s former high street shops, as well as discount supermarket chains Aldi and Lidl, which are understood to be eyeing a selection of UK stores.

Irish family business Henderson Property Group has also expressed interest, further stoking fears that Poundland could be broken up.

A spokesperson for Poundland said: “We understand these kinds of sale processes often lead to significant concern and speculation – much of it wide of the mark.

“We have always had an open door to Usdaw and they know we’re focused on the recovery that’s now firmly embedded in the business.”

Gordon Brothers was contacted for comment.

data.title: ‘An elegant high street for the elite’: Europe’s most magnificent arcades
data.description:
Shopping is as old as cities – and so is the human inclination to enjoy it. Martial’s epigrams satirise the joy of shopping in ancient Rome, while the medieval Frenchman Jean de Jandun described an “insatiable fervour” for browsing the merchandise in Paris’s Les Halles.

But what to do about the rain, mud, sun, dust, rotting butcher’s entrails, pickpockets and prostitutes? The advent of porticos and covered markets, bazaars and exchanges improved the “retail experience” immeasurably, keeping out the rain and also the riff-raff.

In the 1780s, Paris’s Palais-Royal evolved the model further still by creating an arcade: a private street with a roof, thus uniting beauty, comfort and convenience, an elegant high street for the elite. Unsurprisingly, the idea took off.

Europe is now littered with gleaming examples of the grand, elegant shopping arcade – each more beautiful than the last, infinitely worthy of an hour’s pleasant perusing on your next city break (particularly if the heavens open). Here are the best of the bunch.

Leadenhall Market, London (14th century, rebuilt in 1881)

A medieval meat, game and poultry market tamed by the most important Victorian architect you have never heard of, Horace Jones, the designer of Tower Bridge. Jones deployed extravagantly painted cast-iron columns, soaring glass roofs, gas lighting and exuberant decoration to create a colourful fairyland arcade, turning market shopping into modish spectacle. Easily the best City street for your lunchtime sandwich, and a place that draws filmmakers like moths to flame. In Leadenhall’s corner, at 90 Gracechurch Street, a shop’s basement displays part of Roman Londinium’s ancient basilica or covered market. Once a market, always a market?

Burlington Arcade, London (1819)

London’s most charming arcade and the perfect example of turning a problem to your advantage. In 1815, just after the Battle of Waterloo, George Cavendish bought Piccadilly’s Burlington House and discovered a problem. Bond Street’s back gardens overlooked his land, and the inhabitants were chucking oyster shells over the wall. His architect, Samuel Ware, proposed a solution. Why not build a covered arcade and turn the liability into an asset?

It worked. The resulting arcade was charming with a tent-like ceiling and a subtly undulating pattern of arches and shopfront designs. The estate rapidly let all 55 shops and achieved its returns. Bombed in 1940, Burlington Arcade was carefully restored. It flourishes to this day.

Galerie Vivienne, Paris (1826)

Not Paris’s oldest covered shopping arcade, but nevertheless its best. It is intimate not elaborate, a jewel not a jewel box. It is also very French. The neoclassical arcade is elegantly discreet and the mosaic floors quietly exquisite. Thankfully a recent restoration rehabilitated lost ornament. This year marks the Galerie’s second centenary. It is still doing what it always has: selling luxuries to the elite at reassuringly exorbitant prices. In 1986, Jean Paul Gaultier opened a boutique there. Of course he did.

Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert, Brussels (1847)

This was Europe’s first monumental, glazed arcade and a land-assembly masterclass. The scheme’s private backers spent nine years disentangling property rights at the city’s heart – so complicated a process that, en route, one owner reputedly died of a stroke. Another slit his throat.

But it was worth the wait. With a design partly based on Florence’s Uffizi, the arcade was inaugurated by King Leopold, under the motto omnibus omnia, or “everything for everybody”. It was an instant success and has flourished ever since. The owners descend from the galleries’ founders. Continuity pays.

Passage, St Petersburg, Russia (1848)

Imperial Russia did not like being outdone by Paris or London, and the Passage on St Petersburg’s Nevsky Prospect was an expensive exercise in keeping up with the Joneses. Its galleries, shops and café kept out the cold and were glamorous and fashionable in pre-revolutionary St Petersburg. Converted into a “palace of Soviet trade” after the revolution, the Passage miraculously survived the Siege of Leningrad and is today part of a women’s department store. Visiting is off the cards just now, of course.

Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, Milan (1877)

The world’s greatest shopping arcade gets everything right: location, innovation and beautification. Linking Milan’s cathedral with her opera house, La Scala, it brilliantly deployed Victorian glass and iron know-how to span soaring distances. It is also scintillatingly beautiful, with glazed vaults, marble floors and magnificently ornamented façades.

The genesis was difficult, however. Its architect, Giuseppe Mengoni, who had learnt his trade on the railways, proved controversial; the English contractors went bust; and, tragically, Mengoni died falling from the scaffolding a few days before the opening. Nevertheless, the city’s salotto buono, or fine drawing room, was an immediate success, and is one of Europe’s greatest public interiors. Commerce was never more ennobled.

Cross and County arcades, Leeds (1900)

We should remember the delightful Victorian arcades in British towns and cities – we too seldom do, and many are sorely neglected as a result. Two of the most ornate and charming were designed in Leeds by the brilliant theatre architect Frank Matcham and have been lovingly restored. “Come buy, come buy!” they sing under their glass barrel vault. You certainly should.

Nicholas Boys Smith is the founder and chairman of Create Streets and a visiting professor of architecture at the University of Strathclyde

data.title: Trump wants to replace press pool with swimming pool
data.description:
Donald Trump wants to turn the White House press briefing room into a swimming pool and kick reporters out of the West Wing.

The US president has repeatedly discussed plans to move the press out of the White House, according to The New York Times.

The James S Brady press briefing room does sit on the site of a swimming pool, built during Franklin D Roosevelt’s presidency.

Mr Trump pitched the idea to Karoline Leavitt, the former press secretary, as something which could be “her last legacy”, the newspaper reported.

He raised the proposal several times during the final months of her tenure, according to three people with knowledge of the discussions, before she left in August.

Mr Trump has previously floated the idea of turning the briefing room into a swimming pool.

On Sept 27, he shared two images on Truth Social. One showed the briefing room as it is now, captioned “Fake News”, while another showed the space as a swimming pool, captioned “FDR Pool”.

Bill Pulte, the director of the federal housing finance agency who often spends weekends with Mr Trump at his golf clubs, has also been a prominent advocate of the proposal, according to the NYT.

Mr Pulte has even produced a foam-board rendering of the briefing room converted into a pool area, the newspaper reported.

“From the moment I arrived in the White House, I believed it was a national security threat to have the press literally surround the Oval Office,” Steve Bannon told the NYT this month.

He said he had devised a plan to move reporters either off campus, next to Blair House, or to the Eisenhower Executive Office Building.

“But definitely physically remove them from the West Wing,” he said. “That plan landed with a thud among all the other senior advisers to the president.”

In September, The Wall Street Journal reported that Mr Trump had repeatedly discussed moving the press corps out of the White House, but that his advisers had either pushed back or waited for him to abandon the idea.

“America is rightly distrustful of the fake news media because they fabricate stories based off lies and sources who are not even privy to any type of information,” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, said.

“All options remain on the table and we will make an announcement when appropriate.”

data.title: ‘Ozempic face’ powers revival of a fading British giant
data.description:
A surprise discovery may have saved one of Britain’s oldest chemical companies from sliding into irrelevance.

Croda, founded more than 100 years ago, was once known as the “mini ICI”, a powerhouse industrial giant with 70 factories in Lancashire and Yorkshire.

But like so much of Britain’s chemical industry, its star has been fading in recent years.

A share price rally during Covid – after it teamed up with Pfizer to produce one of the first vaccines – has been fizzling out, with its stock declining for four consecutive years.

Now, however, a surprise discovery is reversing Croda’s fortunes, giving the biotech-to-chemicals group a new lease of life as a beauty giant.

Croda recently discovered that one of its old chemicals can be used to treat “Ozempic face”, the often alarming facial transformation associated with the fat-jab craze.

For about a decade, Croda had been producing a skin-plumping chemical derived from the root of the plant anemarrhena to limited sale success.

Known as Volufiline, the agent swells the skin by chemically expanding fat cells and is used mostly in body creams.

But after users of GLP-1 drugs complained of hollow cheeks and sunken eyes, doctors discovered that Volufiline can combat the gaunt features associated with rapid weight loss.

The discovery has led to an explosion of sales for Croda, turning Volufiline into a TikTok sensation, in demand from the French and South Korean cosmetics industry.

Steve Foots, Croda’s chief executive, said the success of Volufiline had taken everybody by surprise.

“It had been in our portfolio for a decade,” he admits. “Ozempic coming on the market has created a big opportunity, which we’re capitalising on. It can lead to facial hollowing, but we can innovate around that by plumping your skin.”

Revenue from Volufiline sales jumped 270pc in the first half as more than 150 companies signed up to use it in their products.

Videos tagged #Volufiline have also generated 200 million views on the US TikTok Shop app in 12 months.

It has prompted Croda to lean into its new profile as a key force in the burgeoning TikTok influencer economy, helping send shares up 25pc from their August 2025 nadir.

Unlike Botox, Volufiline is applied as a face cream or in a lipstick-style tube.

Estée Lauder, the cosmetics giant, is hooked and has started selling a 92pc concentrate version of Croda’s agent under the Volufiline name.

Croda has even managed to sell it to the Korean “K-beauty” industry, which pioneered the skin-transforming agents and exports $11bn (£8.3bn) every year.

Foots said that while the fat-jabs windfall was unexpected, it had resulted from a decades-long repositioning of Croda from traditional chemicals into a supplier to customers, including L’Oréal, Procter & Gamble and Unilever, as well as Estée Lauder.

Next up is hair care. Alongside Volufiline, Croda is pushing KeraBio, a synthetic form of biotech-derived keratin, as its next miracle product.

While Volufiline was an existing ingredient that found a new use, Foots said KeraBio – developed at Croda’s research facility in Daresbury, Cheshire – will be its “first big product launch in the beauty industry”.

A similar serum from an American rival sells for £80 a shot.

“It’s solving the problem of repairing hair that’s been damaged through combing and heating and colouring, which breaks the keratin bonds,” Foots said.

“It strengthens your hair in a chemical way by creating new bonds, and stops it from ageing, which is a bit of a holy grail in the industry.”

For Croda’s proud British roots, its re-emergence as a cosmetics force is a major boost for the nation’s chemicals sector.

Foots said that while Croda’s business was driven by breakthroughs made at a plant in Daresbury and a second research lab at its headquarters near Goole, East Yorkshire, still not enough was being done to make the UK a chemical powerhouse.

Only 950 of Croda’s 5,500 employees are UK based, and while it has three British plants, most production takes place at factories scattered around Europe, the United States and Asia.

While the beauty industry may be Croda’s new frontier, the firm is also expanding the plant in Leek, Staffordshire, that was so critical in producing lipids used to deliver the Pfizer jab.

A recent breakthrough by Moderna and Merck in developing a melanoma vaccine that uses the same mRNA gene therapy principles shows the potential of the sector, Foots said.

He said: “We were prominent in solving the biggest medical crisis of a generation with the biggest innovation of its time, which was gene therapy drugs. And it’s still advancing.

“Flu vaccines, cancer treatments. The science is there. It will take time to get to market, but we’re excited because Croda is provital in many of these programmes.”

Croda may be one of the few independent British chemicals groups still standing, but its Ozempic discovery proves there’s life in the old dog yet.

data.title: Grid staff accuse bosses of covering up blackout risks
data.description:
Engineers running Britain’s electricity grid have accused their bosses of misrepresenting the risk of blackouts, an independent report has found.

The National Energy Systems Operator (Neso) issued a press release in June insisting that the electricity network’s stability was never “at risk” throughout a record-breaking heatwave, despite a strain on supplies.

But an investigation into claims of a cover-up, published on Monday, shows that staff working in Neso’s control room saw this as misleading and felt “frustration” at what they regarded as an understatement of the situation.

It describes a “significant disconnect” between frontline staff and senior executives, whom it is alleged lacked an understanding of operational realities and created “pressure to convey a positive message”.

The investigation report pointed to the press release on June 23 as a key example. While the public statement claimed the system was “not at risk, it was perceived internally by staff as ‘misrepresenting the situation’.”

“Some witnesses expressed the view that the press release should not have stated that the system was ‘not at risk’, when the system was consistently in breach of operational limits for a number of hours, with operators working around the clock to regain balance,” investigators wrote.

Responding to the findings, Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said he had “no confidence” in Fintan Slye, the Neso chief executive, and Paul Golby, the quango’s chairman.

Mr Bowie said: “This report describes a cover-up culture and fears that people in the control room felt they couldn’t raise their concerns.

“It certainly does not let people like Fintan Slye and Paul Golby off the hook – I have no confidence in Neso’s leadership whatsoever.”

The report, produced by law firm Eversheds Sutherlands, ruled on Monday that there was no evidence that there had been “inappropriate influence over operational decisions” at Neso, or that records had been deliberately altered or mismanaged.

But it warned there were nevertheless “high levels of stress and concern” among grid operators “given the challenges of the net zero transition and increased reliance on renewables”, with staff feeling under pressure to avoid creating “bad press.”

The review referred to multiple witnesses who claimed Neso executives did not understand “the reality of the pressures faced by those responsible for keeping the lights on”.

The findings were released as part of an investigation into claims that staff at Neso, a government body backed by the taxpayer, had covered up system failures in June that could have led to blackouts.

Whistleblowers had claimed that grid bosses were “risking blackouts to protect Neso’s reputation”. The allegations were raised in Parliament by Claire Coutinho, the former shadow energy secretary.

Investigators rejected allegations that “control room records were altered or inappropriately managed in any way, including to avoid public scrutiny”.

However, the report warned that staff found it difficult to raise their concerns. The report said: “One witness described an ‘implicit understanding and expectation from the leadership to hear what they want to hear’ and stated that they felt a degree of pressure to convey a positive message, describing the expectation that people make sure ‘everything’s fine’.”

The findings may alarm households and businesses as winter approaches, with suppliers across Europe already battling strained gas supplies caused by the Iran war.

Mr Bowie said: “Far from clearing the heads of Neso or this Labour Government, this report raises more questions than it answers about the culture, management and operational independence of the organisation tasked with keeping the lights on in this country.

“It also confirms what we Conservatives have been saying all along – that the net zero transition and the increased reliance on renewables is making the job of ensuring the grid continues to operate much more difficult, due to the lack of flexibility and inertia in the system.

“We need to end this ideological rush to net zero and DESNZ [the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero] need to radically change how that organisation is run.”

Tim Jarvis, the chief executive of Ofgem, said: “We take the findings of the Eversheds review very seriously. While we note the investigation did not uphold the specific allegations, it raises important and concerning issues about working culture and practices at Neso.”

Mr Slye said he wanted all colleagues “to feel heard”.

Paul Golby, the chairman of Neso, said: “These were serious allegations and the board were explicit that they needed to be investigated independently and comprehensively. We are grateful to everyone who contributed to that work.”

He also acknowledged other issues raised in the report and said he would work to ensure they were addressed as a “matter of urgency”.

‘More questions than answers’

Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said the review “raises areas for cultural improvement in Neso where we expect significant action without delay. We will keep progress under close review.”

The investigation stemmed from claims made by Ms Coutinho earlier this year.

The Tory MP said in July that she had been contacted by whistleblowers who claimed Neso bosses had told staff to stop recording “how key operational decisions are made” during “periods of system stress”.

The whistleblowers alleged that this approach was taken on June 23, when grid operators were forced to issue an alert to power plants driven by fears of tight supplies that evening.

It was also claimed that staff from Neso’s corporate affairs team “interfered in operational decisions” to ensure “stabilising actions were not taken” in a bid to protect the quango’s reputation.

data.title: Grid bosses cling on as investigation lays bare blackout panic
data.description:
When Fintan Slye gathered Britain’s electricity grid staff after whistleblower allegations shook the organisation, he made his feelings about the claims clear.

“There have been a number of allegations in the media, most prominently probably by the shadow secretary of state, Claire Coutinho,” the chief executive of the National Energy System Operator (Neso) said in July. “None of which are true.”

Coutinho had voiced whistleblower concerns in Parliament that grid bosses had covered up just how close Britain came to blackouts during a heatwave on June 23 to protect the organisation’s reputation.

Neso claimed vindication on Monday. An independent investigation by law firm Eversheds Sutherland did not uphold any of the specific allegations surrounding events on June 23.

But far from drawing a line under the matter, the report has only intensified scrutiny of Slye’s leadership.

True, the investigation did not support claims that records had been tampered with, that documents were kept “live” to prevent scrutiny, that corporate affairs staff had meddled in operational decisions or that Neso had breached operational limits and safety constraints.

But those conclusions came with significant caveats.

“The allegations arose for a number of underlying reasons,” lawyers said, “principally, high levels of operational stress, a significant disconnect between the [control room] and executive leadership, a culture of reputational sensitivity affecting the perception of operational independence, and a gap between formal speak up commitments and the lived experience of staff.

“These wider concerns, whilst not establishing any of the four specific allegations, identify control, cultural and governance issues that should be addressed.”

Responding to the findings, Michael Shanks, Labour energy minister, suggested the Tories had been chasing headlines and that “none of the allegations can be substantiated by the evidence”.

But Andrew Bowie, the current shadow energy secretary, said the report raised “more questions than answers”.

“It is difficult to separate allegations of altering records to avoid scrutiny from findings that point to an organisational culture overly focused on reputation management,” he said in a letter to Mr Shanks.

“Equally, it is difficult to divorce allegations of inappropriate corporate affairs involvement in operational decisions from the report’s conclusion that there exists a perception within parts of the control room that senior leadership does not fully understand the realities of operating the grid.

“Rather than disproving the allegations, the report appears to describe the very environment in which such behaviour could arise.”

The law firm’s report painted a picture of an internal culture at Neso where engineers felt they couldn’t raise their fears about the safe operation of the grid. This is despite “high levels of stress and concern” about their ability to keep the lights on.

Engineers complained that balancing the system was becoming harder because of “challenges of the net zero transition”, with conventional coal-fired and gas-fired power plants easier to manage than “less flexible” renewables, which made “the job more difficult”.

Lawyers noted that commenting on net zero was outside their expertise and their remit.

But they warned that engineers felt they had no option but to become whistleblowers because no one was listening to their concerns, even when they raised them through the proper channels.

Some felt Neso was in hock to the Government, which has set a flagship target for Britain to switch to a 90pc “clean” power system by 2030.

“We’ve seen people who put their head above the parapet,” said one witness who spoke to investigating lawyers.

“It doesn’t last very long. They get beaten down, and either they find something else to do or they become very quiescent.”

The Telegraph previously reported that Craig Dyke, Neso’s operations director, told staff that they had been “let down” by whistleblowers who had raised concerns with Coutinho.

Eversheds’s report also warned that engineers felt pressured to hold off on drastic actions for fear of how they would play in the press.

While this didn’t prove “direct interference” by corporate affairs staff, evidence pointed to “a broader culture of sensitivity” in which concerns about how things would look to outsiders were “communicated to operational staff, whether directly, through senior management or through perception”.

One person complained of an “implicit understanding and expectation from the leadership to hear what they want to hear” and pressure to show that “everything’s fine”, while another said they felt a “bias towards presenting good news” came from the top of the organisation.

This affected how willing some staff felt to issue an electricity margin notice (EMN), which asks generators to switch on if backup power is needed, and other market notices, even when things became serious.

Such notices should be issued “without any fear”, one person said, before adding: “Unfortunately we are not in that space.”

EMNs, several of which have already been issued this year, months before winter, were treated as “almost the last resort”.

On one occasion, control room staff were preparing to issue an even more serious “high risk of demand control” (HRDR) notice when a senior manager arrived.

“There was a discussion, and then it wasn’t ... issued,” a witness recalled.

An HRDR notice warns that Neso may need to take emergency action to prevent blackouts, says Kathryn Porter, an independent energy analyst.

The independent report says one was considered on June 23 and again on June 25, during the heatwave.

Neso’s own website describes an HRDR notice as something issued only in “extremely rare and unusual circumstances where forecast demand for electricity is greater than the levels of supply available”.

It can involve lowering voltage so demand is “stretched out”, meaning kettles might boil more slowly, for instance, but it can also involve Neso imposing power cuts if that is also deemed necessary.

“The fact they were considering HRDR is really significant,” says Porter. “It has not happened in years or even decades.

“They would essentially be saying at that point that you have no more tools to increase generation, so to meet demand the only thing you can do is reduce demand.”

Porter pointed to another piece of testimony from an engineer who wasn’t on duty on June 22, but still felt EMN and HRDR notices should have been issued.

They claimed margins were so thin that Neso couldn’t have covered a single unexpected outage, but that notices were withheld because of “optics”.

Other engineers disagreed, however, with one saying the situation wasn’t “anywhere close” to this.

Nonetheless, unease remained about how Neso’s senior managers publicly presented the situation on June 23. Official statements said market notices issued at the time did not “mean electricity supply is at risk” and insisted the system had “operated securely” at all times.

Behind the scenes, control room engineers were in disbelief. The report concluded that staff believed the press releases were “misrepresenting the situation”. The lawyers warned of a “significant disconnect” between staff and senior management.

The quango was “consistently in breach of operational limits for a number of hours, with operators working around the clock to regain balance”, according to the independent report.

Eversheds dismissed claims that documents had been deliberately changed or mismanaged to hide blackout worries. However, they noted that the firm did not retain amended versions of Microsoft Word and Excel logs, meaning edits repeatedly overrode earlier entries.

Neso said it would implement the law firm’s recommendations on Monday, including changes to record-keeping procedures and better channels for staff to raise concerns.

But the report still reads awkwardly for the quango’s bosses, who for now are clinging to their jobs.

Paul Golby, Neso’s chairman, said: “The investigation’s findings are clear that there was no evidence to substantiate any of the allegations around inappropriate influence over decision-making or inappropriate record-keeping processes.

“The board will oversee the development of plans to address the issues raised in the report and ensure these are implemented as a matter of urgency.”

Slye, who was paid more than £700,000 last year, said: “We welcome the findings of [the] independent and rigorous investigation.

“It is constructive in identifying areas where we could improve how colleagues can raise concerns and how we respond to them.

“I want all colleagues at Neso to feel heard.”

data.title: Ministers accused of concealing true scale of England’s green belt loss
data.description:
Ministers have been accused of covering up the true scale of England’s green-belt loss as Labour pushes for more building.

Figures issued by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government this week showed that England’s green belt shrank by just 0.03pc in the year ending March 2026.

However, the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE) said a grey-belt loophole meant swathes of lost land were not being counted in the figures.

Richard Hebditch, the CPRE’s planning representative, said the figures were “misleading” because they ignored the fact that green-belt land could now be built on if it was reclassified as grey belt. This land is not counted as lost in official statistics.

Mr Hebditch said: “Either the Government is happy for [the data] to be largely meaningless or they are deliberately deceitful stats, hiding what is actually happening.

“It doesn’t capture the significant amounts of land that we are losing from the grey-belt policy.”

The grey belt refers to sites in the green belt such as scrub land, disused car parks or petrol stations that are deemed to be of little natural value and instead are ideal for property development.

Under planning reforms made by Angela Rayner, the Housing Secretary, introduced in December 2024, land judged to be grey belt can be built on while remaining officially designated as green belt.

New planning rules introduced in August made it even easier to undertake construction projects near “well-connected” railway stations, including in the green belt.

None of this was included in the Government’s headline numbers.

Its researchers admitted in the report that they could not estimate how much of the green belt had been identified as grey belt and said that statisticians were exploring whether to collect these data.

The Government’s figures only looked at formal changes to green-belt boundaries, which happen when councils draw up new local plans for their areas.

Seven councils did this during the 2025‐26 period, with Tunbridge Wells, Kent, losing the most protected land at 220 hectares.

A grey-belt designation does not necessarily mean all of that land will be developed. Nonetheless, Mr Hebditch argued that the figures should be included as the designation opens the door to possible building work on the area.

Figures from Channel 4 News showed that 96pc of protected land in Guildford, Surrey, was potentially grey belt, alongside 92pc in Stoke-on-Trent and nearly 80pc in Solihull, West Midlands.

“There is a real lack of transparency to communities about what will be happening to land around their towns and villages,” Mr Hebditch said.

“It’s important for them to know what effect the policy changes are having ... and what’s actually being decided about the use of that land.”

The Government’s 0.03pc estimate compares with a 0.04pc loss of green belt land in the previous year.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government has been contacted for comment.

data.title: Property giant halts £3.6bn development project
data.description:
One of Britain’s largest property firms has paused construction at a £3.6bn development in London as it struggles to find buyers for its apartments.

British Land, listed on the FTSE 100, will not go ahead with the second phase of construction in Canada Water, south-east London, as the company grapples with rising costs and sluggish sales.

The property group is understood to be waiting for a clear improvement in market conditions before resuming work on the project’s mix of homes, offices and retail spaces.

The decision is another blow to the capital’s housebuilding industry, amid a steep decline in construction and claims that the market is “fundamentally broken”.

The first phase of British Land’s 53-acre development at Canada Water includes 245,000 sq ft of offices, along with 186 new homes at a project called The Founding. Nearly 80 affordable homes are also included in the development.

Approval has been granted for up to 4,184 new homes on the site, but in its annual report released in May this year, British Land said it had sold just 57 apartments.

It also admitted that challenging market conditions, difficulties with leases and sales, as well as changes to the development had caused the project’s valuation to fall by 6.9pc in the last financial year.

British Land jointly funds the development alongside pension fund AustralianSuper. Both companies have been contacted for comment.

The decision brings one of London’s largest regeneration projects to a halt, at a time when London is on course to build just 20pc of the Government’s annual homes target of 88,000, according to figures from Molior.

In recent months, a succession of property developers has warned that London is becoming increasingly unviable for new house-building projects.

Landsec shelved a £1.5bn plan this week to rebuild a shopping centre and create 1,700 new homes in Lewisham, south-east London, after the borough’s Green-led council demanded more affordable housing.

Jennie Daly, the boss of housebuilder Taylor Wimpey, also said this month that building in the capital was “fundamentally broken”, and that the incentive to take on risky projects had “evaporated”.

Berkeley, another major housebuilder, recently said it was grappling with “extreme uncertainty” after authorities delayed or blocked plans for thousands of new London homes across different projects.

Buyers are struggling with mortgage costs which have increased rapidly since the start of the Iran war, while construction companies are feeling the pinch from rising material costs.

It comes after home completions across England dropped to their lowest level since 2016.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics show that 142,050 new homes were completed in England in 2025, a nine-year low.

The slowdown in housebuilding casts further doubt on Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledge to build 1.5 million new homes by the end of the decade.

data.title: Winter blackout risk rises for first time since 2022
data.description:
The risk of winter blackouts has risen for the first time in four years, amid warnings from Britain’s grid operator that net zero is making it harder to keep the lights on.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso) said on Friday that the forecast power buffer to protect the country from winter blackouts would be 5.9 gigawatts (GW), or 9.5pc of demand.

That compares with 6.1GW, or 10pc, last year.

It marks the first drop in the so-called de-rated margin, the projected amount of spare power during a cold spell, since the outbreak of the Ukraine war in 2022.

Neso said increased electricity demand had squeezed the margin. This may be coming from energy-hungry data centres, as well as rising household adoption of electric cars and heat pumps.

A damning independent report earlier this week warned that Neso control-room engineers were concerned that the switch to renewable energy was making it harder to manage the grid but felt pressure to “convey a positive message”.

The quango, responsible for the day-to-day management of Britain’s power system, stressed on Friday that supplies were still “sufficient for the forthcoming winter” and “expected to remain secure”.

However, the top civil servant in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero admitted to MPs that the Government could not rule out blackouts.

Jonathan Brearley, the permanent secretary, told members of the public accounts committee: “We can never guarantee the lights won’t go out.

“As you know, there are always risks in any system.”

This winter’s safeguard figure was calculated using a different methodology to last year’s. The new methodology assigns wind farms a higher level of reliability.

Under the previous methodology, the margin would have been 5.2GW, or 8.4pc of demand.

Britain’s total power-generation capacity has grown from 127GW to 137GW in the past year. However, much of the increase comes from renewables, which are less reliable than other power sources such as gas and nuclear.

As a result, Neso cannot bank on the expanded capacity to provide a larger safety cushion.

‘There are always going to be risks’

The quango’s forecasts that Britain’s power will remain secure during the winter rest on the assumption it can call on European neighbours for help.

Without electricity imports from the Continent on the coldest winter days, the margin would be wiped out.

Mr Brearley said the Government may struggle to upgrade the grid sufficiently by 2030 to meet its pledge to power Britain with clean energy.

He told MPs: “We’ve got to recognise that there are always going to be risks around a programme this big.

“Some of those are within our control or the network company’s control, and some of those are outside of it.

“In this system, ultimately, the transmission companies are responsible for making sure these are delivered on time.”

Tim Jarvis, the chief executive of energy watchdog Ofgem, also said when pressed on the issue: “We accept there is risk there.”

Deborah Petterson, the director of resilience at Neso, said: “Despite continued geopolitical uncertainty and volatility in global energy markets, Britain enters this winter with a resilient and well-prepared electricity system.

“Our winter outlook shows we have sufficient margins and a diverse mix of generation sources to meet demand, even during periods of colder weather and higher system stress.

“While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain’s electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world.”

Separately, a winter outlook published by National Gas on Friday similarly predicted Britain’s supplies would be secure but cautioned that prices might surge.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Grid blackout warnings cannot be dismissed as scaremongering
data.description:
It’s becoming fashionable to dismiss warnings about electricity blackouts as scaremongering. Yet two reports published this week raise serious questions about the security of Britain’s electricity grid, while a succession of incidents this month suggests the problems are far from resolved.

On June 23, grid frequency fell below its normal operating range for an extended period. Frequency is essentially a measure of supply versus demand. The two must be balanced to ensure a stable electricity grid.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso) sought emergency assistance from neighbouring countries, while five constraints on the transmission network were breached.

An independent investigation by lawyers Eversheds Sutherland into allegations made by Neso whistleblowers concluded that none of the four specific allegations investigated was substantiated. Ministers have seized on this finding, but the detail of the report makes for uncomfortable reading.

Investigators uncovered weaknesses in operational record-keeping, concerns about management culture and evidence that engineers were reluctant to issue market warnings because of the reputational consequences for Neso.

One witness described engineers as increasingly risk-averse about issuing electricity margin notices, which warn the market that there may be insufficient power generation available. These notices exist specifically to encourage generators to make additional capacity available so that there is enough electricity to meet demand. Their issuance should be determined by engineering and energy-supply considerations, not worries about embarrassing the organisation.

The investigation revealed that engineers had changed a spreadsheet used to calculate whether more serious warnings were needed. The spreadsheet would otherwise have indicated that a “high risk of demand reduction” warning should be issued – a warning that, in a worst-case scenario, could lead to power cuts.

Eversheds accepted explanations that these adjustments were technically justified. But why are critical decisions about electricity security being made using manually adjusted Excel spreadsheets, rather than properly controlled operational software? Important operational logs were also missing for that week, but Eversheds did not establish why they had not been produced or whether they might subsequently have been deleted.

The report records conflicting evidence about whether Neso had enough reserves to withstand the sudden loss of a major electricity generator or interconnector.

One witness said the control room could not cover the loss of its largest generator; others said it could. That’s not a minor disagreement: maintaining sufficient reserves is fundamental to grid security. There should be no doubt at all about whether this requirement was met.

Neso’s own preliminary report acknowledges that it had exhausted all available and commercially accessible actions to keep the grid balanced, while frequency remained outside normal range. It also confirmed that five transmission constraints were exceeded despite having strongly implied to the media over the summer they had not.

And it admitted to material forecasting errors on electricity demand and wind power supply. This used up reserves that would otherwise protect against unexpected failures.

Ofgem has not concluded that the grid was secure. Its technical investigation remains ongoing.

Meanwhile, more recent events have provided further cause for concern.

On Oct 6, low wind output prompted a margin warning and expensive emergency balancing actions. On Oct 12, Neso sought substantial emergency assistance from France despite demand being well below typical winter peaks. On Oct 14, interconnector trading limits were repeatedly exceeded and balancing costs approached £50m in a single day.

The underlying problem is that Britain’s electricity system is becoming increasingly complex and difficult to manage.

Wind generation is often located far from demand centres, while grid constraints prevent electricity moving freely around the country. Falling inertia, a force usually provided by spinning generators in conventional gas power plants, creates stability challenges.

Ageing gas-fired power stations remain essential during periods of low wind, while Britain is increasingly dependent on electricity imports that neighbouring countries cannot be compelled to provide.

At the same time, Neso continues to rely on ageing software, vulnerable communications systems and manual processes. Eversheds identified high levels of stress among control room staff and a culture in which experienced operators had either left or stopped raising concerns.

Electricity security is not measured by whether the lights stayed on yesterday – it’s measured by whether the system can withstand the failures that might reasonably occur tomorrow.

With so many identifiable risks, worrying about blackouts is not scaremongering. Dismissing those concerns without properly addressing them is the bigger danger.

data.title: Fashion isn’t art – but at least it hasn’t given up on beauty
data.description:
I am not saying that my Ralph Lauren quarter-zip or your Isabel Marant Priyanka wool jumper are comparable to Michelangelo. I am not even saying that they are comparable to John Sell Cotman, a minor English watercolourist.

What I am saying is that “art” today is so vacuous, inane and banal, supported by gibberish from too many useful idiots, that fashion is not quite as frivolous as it once seemed.

True, Coco Chanel said “fashion is what goes out of fashion”, but at least fashion reminds us that art must have a connection to pleasure. That’s not a connection you would find in the utterly barren bloviation of the reliably ludicrous Turner Prize.

Fashion is a branch of design. And design is the application of intelligence and taste to raw materials. The 2024 Turner Prize winner draped an over-sized doily over a Ford Escort. Believe me, there was more art in the humble car before it was molested by lofty pretension.

Design is what turns meaningless stone, bricks, iron and glass into exalting architecture. We may soon have had quite enough of the motor car, but it’s nonetheless true that people learn about the emotional effect of colour, form and symbolism from looking at cars.

Fashion and design are not quite art, but they have usurped art’s role in culture. This is because artists have vacated the space they once occupied in the popular imagination. And their vacation has taken them to places no one wants to go.

Fashion and design are about democracy. They must be accessible, or they will fail. And that accessibility has to be real. Art that is of interest to a handful of people is not art at all. We need another name for what the Turner Prize encourages.

Even to be having a debate on “can fashion be art” is a vivid illustration not so much of the power of fashion as of the abject poverty of contemporary art. And the obscenity of the “art world”. Here please note that when the word “world” is used as a suffix, as in Caravan World, for example, it does not signify global relevance.

On the contrary, it suggests a tight and myopic community of plutocrats showing-off. As Kurt Vonnegut remarked in Breakfast of Champions, the art world is “a conspiracy with millionaires to make poor people feel stupid”.

The great thing about comfortingly analogue fashion and design is that, at their best, they dignify the consumer. They enhance senses of well-being and life’s purposes. No one can say that about the ugly atrocities of, say, the Chapman brothers whose crude desire to shock is juvenile.

Of course, shocking can be good. Goya and Grünewald painted shocking pictures, but they had finesse… as well as intelligence and taste. The problem with the Chapmans is not that their mutants and cadavers are shocking, but that they are… boring. Let me say it: contemporary art is all boring. Fashion is not.

The New York designer Milton Glaser created the ineffable, ubiquitous and widely imitated “I HEART NY” device. In 1989 he told me: “The most significant value of any work of art or design is in its effect on the world.”

Never a truer word. These things can’t be quantified, but Glaser’s inspired graphics are surely more popular than Damien Hirst’s clever pranks.

Of course, I can anticipate my defence of fashion and design being dismissed as a liking for (mere) “popular culture”. But lazy thinkers use that term to protect ultramontane “high art” from competition by designers who are engaged with the world out there, its appetites and dreams.

Tom Wolfe’s mischievous baiting of Literary America is pure gold in the conversation about high and low art. John Updike scorned Wolfe, author of the epochal Bonfire of the Vanities, as not being literature, but “entertainment”. That is hilariously revealing of the qualities Updike thought literature should aspire to.

Wolfe himself wrote a brilliantly combative essay called “Chester Gould versus Roy Lichtenstein”, Chester Gould being the illustrator of the popular Dick Tracy cartoons, Roy Lichtenstein being the “artist” who parodied him.

Wolfe convinced me (and most readers) that Chester Gould was the superior talent.

I live only a short walk from Tate Britain whose current exhibition about fashion and art in Nineties Britain has incensed even The Guardian by its slack fatuity. The problem is not the claims it makes for fashion to be taken seriously, but its refusal to engage in finer thoughts.

Me? I haven’t been. I love art and I’ll find more of it in the nearby Ferrari dealer. Meanwhile, collecting art is beyond the means of the 99 per cent. Collecting clothes is not.

data.title: Labour peer lined up as new Thames Water chairman
data.description:
Thames Water’s lenders have lined up a Labour peer to chair the company as Andy Burnham pushes to take public control of the embattled utility.

Lord Hutton, a former Cabinet minister, will become the most senior figure at Thames if a consortium of creditors succeeds in its £10bn rescue bid for the group.

London & Valley Water said Lord Hutton would be installed as chairman if its ownership bid succeeds, supported by telecoms veteran Mike McTighe who was named vice-chairman.

Hiring Lord Hutton may placate some Labour figures opposed to the creditors’ ownership of Thames.

The 71-year old held several senior roles between 1997 and 2010, serving as work and pensions secretary in Sir Tony Blair’s government and business secretary and then defence secretary under Gordon Brown.

However, as a staunch Blairite, Lord Hutton admitted to privately briefing that Mr Brown would be “a f------ disaster” if he became prime minister. The comments were made in 2006 when Sir Tony was facing an internal coup from Mr Brown and his supporters.

London & Valley Water’s move comes as the group of lenders attempts to head off Mr Burnham’s calls to bring water companies into public ownership.

The creditors are finalising a revised £10bn rescue deal it hopes will win over Ofwat, the regulator. The proposal is expected to be tabled in the next few weeks.

However, the environment, food and rural affairs select committee urged the Government to reject the plan last week.

The news of Lord Hutton’s appointment comes as the Prime Minister looks for alternative ways to bring Thames under public control.

Mr Burnham has reportedly ordered government officials to come up with more radical solutions for how to address the debacle at Britain’s largest water company, according to The Guardian.

He has previously expressed support for nationalising Thames Water. However, it is thought the Prime Minister has been warned that the Government cannot afford to do so.

Mr Burnham has been unable to find a way to bring the company under public control without spending billions in taxpayer money or risk getting caught up in a drawn out legal battle.

Officials believe that changes to the “special administration regime” would make it less challenging for the Government to take firms such as Thames Water into state control in the coming years.

Another idea is for the Government to forgo £100m of fines owed by Thames in return for a stake in the group.

Lord Hutton said: “People living in London and the Thames Valley have the right to expect the highest possible standards of customer service and proper environmental stewardship from their water company, and that will be our focus as we look to the future.”

London & Valley Water was created by a group of fund managers, including Apollo Global Management, Elliott Management, Farallon Capital Management and Silver Point Capital. They have already lent the stricken company £3bn to keep it afloat.

The lenders collectively hold £17bn of Thames Water’s £21bn debt pile.

data.title: Households face higher bills to guard against threat of gas shortages
data.description:
British households will pay more on their gas bills to safeguard against shortages amid concerns about a backup pipeline to Europe.

Ofgem, the energy regulator, said on Thursday that bills needed to rise to pay for the maintenance costs of an undersea gas interconnector linking the UK and Belgium.

Without the pipeline, it warned that the grid would risk gas shortages in a worst-case winter scenario where temperatures plummet and a major system failure happens elsewhere.

That could leave power plants without enough fuel or – in extreme circumstances – households without their central heating.

The Belgian link can funnel up to 73 million cubic metres of gas a day into Britain’s network during an emergency – about 15pc to 20pc of the country’s needs when demand is highest.

But Interconnector Limited, its owner, has been scaling back capacity in recent years as it is used less often and as the equipment ages, making it more costly to maintain and keep on standby.

As a result, National Gas – which runs Britain’s main gas transmission system – requested permission to pay more money to keep the pipeline in working order to maintain its capacity.

It must secure permission from Ofgem to do this because the costs are ultimately shouldered by households and businesses, through their bills.

Ofgem said the change was expected to add about £1.19 to a typical household’s annual gas bill, or about 10p per month.

The regulator stressed that there was no immediate risk to the gas system but said keeping the pipeline in play was essential to guaranteeing security of supplies in the event of a crisis.

It said: “While these pipelines are only used occasionally to import gas into Great Britain, they provide an important option during periods of particularly high demand, such as severe winter weather.”

The decision underscores the growing importance of European imports to Britain’s energy security as domestic gas production in the North Sea continues to decline.

Britain has been a net importer of gas since 2004, with about half of supplies coming from overseas today.

This includes about 40pc from European pipelines and 13pc via ocean-going tankers full of liquefied natural gas from countries such as the United States and Qatar.

Glenn Bryn-Jacobsen, of National Gas, said: “While the gas market continues to provide secure supplies under normal conditions, recent analysis has identified some very unlikely but potentially high-impact stress scenarios where additional resilience measures could be beneficial.

“Maintaining import capability through the Continental interconnectors has been identified as an important action to strengthen resilience.”

Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said: “We are working with industry to build a gas system fit for the future, ensuring value for money for consumers while giving investors’ confidence to back Britain’s energy sector.”

However, the Conservatives claimed on Monday that policies imposed by Mr Shanks and the Labour administration were partly to blame for the situation.

Since coming to power in 2024, Labour has vowed not to grant new licences for oil and gas exploration and imposed higher windfall taxes on North Sea producers, leading to warnings that the industry is being pushed into “accelerated decline”.

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said: “The National Gas grid cannot guarantee that homes will be warm, lights come on or industry function on a peak day this winter.

“And why? Because of an accelerated decline in domestic gas supply from the North Sea.

“So what is the solution? For British bill-payers to pay more, to import more from Europe (specifically Belgium) to keep the lights on in Britain.”

The news comes a day after Andy Burnham signed off on drilling of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, a move that could bring it online within weeks.

data.title: Jet engine jobs to stay in UK after taxpayers hand factory £33m
data.description:
General Electric (GE) will receive up to £33m of taxpayer funding to encourage the US aerospace giant to keep jet-engine maintenance jobs in the UK.

The money from the UK, Scottish and local governments will safeguard 850 existing posts at Prestwick, on the Ayrshire coast, and create 150 new positions, the company said on Monday.

Andy Prow, the Prestwick plant’s manager, said that without the funding GE could have expanded at overseas sites with lower labour costs. GE is backing the plant with £30m of its own money.

While Prestwick maintains 50pc of all GE engines for Boeing’s best-selling 787 jet, the firm also has sites in Brazil and Taiwan that repair the turbines, as well as a facility in Poland.

Mr Prow said: “The other sites are in a lower cost-type environment. That’s something we’ll never be able to compete with.

“Getting government funding and partnership is critical to ensuring that GE continues to see the UK, Scotland and Prestwick as an area they want to work in.

“Otherwise it’s a really difficult package to present when you’re competing against other global workshops. Let’s not kid ourselves; other global facilities and countries have got investment and tax benefits.”

The money will fund a 5,110 sq m building, increasing the size of the Prestwick plant by about 20pc.

Mr Prow said further expansion may be required, as the Boeing 787 is not expected to reach peak production until the late 2030s, and that “partnerships” with the Government would remain vital.

While the investment will also support supply-chain jobs, the £33m public-fund outlay to secure 150 new posts highlights the challenge facing Andy Burnham after he pledged to reindustrialise Britain and foster growth in every postcode.

Reuben Aitken, the head of international investment at Scottish Enterprise, said it would be misguided to lavish money on reviving dinosaur industries and that the Government should be prepared to pick winners.

He said: “To expand the industrial base, we need a really ruthless focus on areas where we can be globally competitive. The mission-based approach of getting behind a limited number of key priorities is backed up by all the economic evidence.

“We’re in a globally competitive world. Spreading the jam too thin is never the way to go. You have to pick what you’re going after, wrap support around it and lean into those strengths.”

Melanie Ward, the Scotland minister, said Prestwick needed financial backing because the site “hasn’t always had a certain future”.

She said reindustrialisation was “about looking to the future, not the past”, and in Scotland would centre on defence, green energy and nuclear power, “if the Scottish Government would allow it”.

Ms Ward said: “There are potentially thousands of highly skilled jobs to come in nuclear, but we currently have ideological opposition preventing that and cutting off opportunities.”

Jenny Gilruth, the Deputy First Minister of Scotland, said the Scottish National Party would look at projects on a case-by-case basis and that “creating the conditions for GE to stay” had been a vital step.

She added that the SNP remains against nuclear power “and we won’t support that”.

data.title: Scrap ‘delusional’ electric car sales targets, Renault boss says
data.description:
The carmaker behind one of Britain’s most popular electric vehicles (EVs) has urged ministers to scale back “delusional” net zero targets amid fears they risk backfiring.

Adam Wood, the boss of Renault UK, insisted the French automotive giant supported the green transition and pointed to booming sales of the Renault 5 electric hatchback as proof that consumers would buy affordable cars.

However, he warned that the trajectory of the Government’s zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate was so steep that it was becoming “unsustainable” and could force manufacturers to scale back investment in EV technologies.

Speaking at the company’s office in north-west London, Mr Wood told The Telegraph: “For us, the debate is not the destination – we are absolutely convinced the destination is 100pc electric.

“The debate is about the speed at which we get there.

“But we shouldn’t be complacent or delusional that we have something today that is absolutely aligned with the ZEV mandate because we don’t.”

Mr Wood said consumer demand had “not kept pace with the ZEV mandate” and was being propped up by “unsustainable levels” of discounting by manufacturers.

He added: “The trajectory needs to be sustainable for the industry at a time when, let’s not forget, manufacturers are having to invest more than ever in the next generation of technology to make that transition happen.

“Anything that puts in jeopardy that investment – and the certainty that the automotive industry needs more than ever – is unhelpful.”

Ministers are reviewing the ZEV mandate following intense lobbying by carmakers, who say they are struggling to keep up.

Renault’s call to relax the rules will sound alarm bells in Whitehall because the company is one of the few that has managed to stay ahead of the targets.

This year’s headline requirement is for 33pc of cars sold to be electric.

Mr Wood said the French manufacturer’s sales are “approaching 50pc” thanks to the success of the revamped Renault 5. That compares with an overall market share of 26pc for electric cars so far this year.

At the same time, Renault has seen a “seismic” jump in EV sales since the outbreak of the US-Iran war, which has sent petrol and diesel prices soaring to record highs, Mr Wood said.

“People are doing the maths,” he said, pointing to analysis showing electric drivers could save £600 a year on fuel.

However, the ZEV mandate target will rise to 38pc of vehicle output in 2027, 52pc in 2028, 66pc in 2029 and 80pc in 2030. Mr Wood said even Renault was worried about meeting it in later years.

He pointed to ongoing driver concerns about the cost and extensiveness of public charging networks, adding: “You’ve got to have an eye on the future because 50pc today is not 80pc in 2030.”

He added that the escalating requirements of the ZEV mandate were not on a “linear curve – it’s an exponential one”.

“We’ve started to demonstrate that when you create a virtuous circle of affordability – accessible vehicles, improving charging infrastructure and a cost of ownership equation which works for people – then you can convert more people to go electric,” he said. “But that doesn’t mean that with a market at 26pc today, we’re on course sustainably to be at 80pc by 2030.”

The targets for electric light commercial vans (LCVs) were particularly challenging, he said.

“The LCV market today is hovering around 10pc for EVs but we’re talking about 70pc by 2030.”

Mr Wood argued that the Renault 5 – which comes in a striking shade of yellow by default – had been successful because it “brought electric cars into a more affordable space” while also “bringing a smile to people’s faces”.

Unlike many other EVs launched by Western brands, it is a small car rather than an SUV, putting it squarely up against the likes of Chinese competitors such as the BYD Dolphin.

“I think the industry, perhaps in pursuit of electrification, has sometimes been guilty of potentially trying to sell a category of vehicles to customers,” Mr Wood said.

“What we’ve come back to is the core of what motivates people to buy. It’s not simply a rational choice, it’s one that’s also emotional.”

The four-door hatchback, which sells for as little as £21,495 after a government grant, was the UK’s most popular EV in April and July this year.

Since its launch in January 2025, almost 20,000 have been sold in the UK, including 10,000 so far this year.

It has helped Renault to grow sales in 2026 while rivals including Ford, Volkswagen and Fiat have flagged.

Mr Wood, a father of two, owns a Renault 5 himself – along with a Renault Scenic SUV – but he admits: “I struggle to prize it away from my wife. They’re great fun to drive.”

Before the end of this year, Renault will also launch the smaller and lower-priced Twingo electric city car for sale in the UK.

It is expected to cost less than £20,000 – or potentially as little as £16,000 after a government grant, should it qualify for the full amount.

That would make it competitive versus even the cheapest cars made by Chinese brands such as BYD and Jaecoo, which have been relentlessly eating into the market shares of Western manufacturers.

“It will be extremely competitive,” Mr Wood said. “The car is really agile and it’s also extremely fun.”

The Twingo was developed in just two years – at “China speed” – because of work carried out by the company’s “advanced China development centre” in Shanghai, where a prototype was built.

Although it was partly designed in China, the vehicle was built on top of a French core design and will be manufactured in Slovenia. The Renault 5 is made in France.

Car development cycles normally take around five years, with Mr Wood arguing that the Twingo’s development was an example of Western carmakers learning how to catch up with their Chinese rivals.

“With Twingo, what we’ve demonstrated is the humility to acknowledge that China is part of the epicentre of global car development, particularly in electric vehicles,” he said.

“That’s what enabled us to break records. We’ve developed a car in two years from concept to reality and brought it to market. Crucially, though, that’s on a platform that was developed in Europe by Renault engineers.

“We’re demonstrating that it is absolutely possible to be competitive [with China]. The Renault 5 is testament to that.”
