data.title: Germany’s battle to break its economic addiction to China turns existential
data.description:
For decades, Germany seemed immune to the China shock that has wreaked havoc on Western manufacturers.

After Beijing joined the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in 2001 and flooded markets with cheap goods, Germany’s carmakers and chemicals producers not only stood strong but benefited from selling to the new Chinese market.

However, German policymakers and industrialists became complacent as China pursued closer business ties. Cue what economists have coined the “China Shock 2.0” and Germany is suddenly one of the most vulnerable countries in the world.

Now, German-China relations are undergoing a sea change as Chancellor Friedrich Merz wakes up to how Beijing’s new era of global dominance is hammering the German economy.

As recently as 2020, Germany had a trade surplus of nearly €20bn (£17bn) with China. This is now a deficit of €21bn.

Analysis by the Global Public Policy Institute shows that while many countries, including the UK, have reduced their exposure to China in recent years, Germany has become increasingly vulnerable. Since 2013, Germany has moved from the 10th most exposed country to China to the third, behind only South Korea and Russia.

In a Centre for European Reform paper earlier this year, economists Sander Tordoir and Brad Setser warned that “China Shock 2.0” is similar in scale to the first one, which followed China’s accession to the WTO in 2001. Back then, China’s manufacturing surplus climbed to nearly 1pc of global GDP. In the last four years, this has grown by almost another percentage point.

But this time the shock is more existential. In the 2000s, when the West lost manufacturers who made toys, furniture and basic electronics, they did not lose sectors that were central to the future dynamism of their economies, Tordoir and Setser argued.

Countries such as Germany also gained major new export markets in chemicals and machinery. This time, China is not increasing its imports. And the sectors that it is now competing with – namely cars, machinery and chemicals – are vitally important to Germany’s economy.

Chinese goods are now not only cheap but high quality and Germany is suddenly seeing its core exports squeezed out of China and other foreign markets, but also at home.

“For years, the German elites told themselves that interdependence meant mutual dependence, but the latest numbers look less comfortable,” says Sari Arho Havrén, a China foreign-relations specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi).

Cars, an industry which Germany has dominated for decades, are at the heart of this second wave of Chinese exports.

Analysts had expected that China would export 10 million cars a year by the end of the decade. But on an annualised basis, China’s car exports hit this threshold in the last three months of 2025.

“In the automobile sector, the tipping point was really when Chinese companies started leading the field in electric vehicles and hybrid cars,” says Jessie Yin, associate director at the Atlantic Council’s Geoeconomics Centre.

This is one reason why China’s export volumes last year grew at more than double the pace of global trade.

As China’s star ascends, Germany is left flailing. Its exports have been falling steadily since 2018 and dropped by around 5pc last year. The industries most exposed to Chinese competition have been shrinking most markedly. Its industrial production has been falling for six years and economic output is still around 6pc below its pre-pandemic trajectory.

Tordoir and Setser, of the Centre for European Reform, warn: “China shock is now the most important cause of Germany’s malaise.”

It has much further to fall. A report published earlier this year by the French prime minister’s planning office warned Chinese competition could threaten 70pc of Germany’s manufacturing output over the medium term.

Merz is now trying to claw back control.

On his first visit as chancellor to Beijing in February, Merz warned that Germany’s trade deficit with China had quadrupled in five years, diagnosing it as “not healthy”. He has warned several times of signs that China is manipulating its currency.

This month, in a joint letter with Emmanuel Macron, the French president, he called on Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to bring in a mechanism to allow the EU to impose faster restrictions on countries engaging in harmful trade practices.

And just last week, Germany blocked Chinese state-owned shipping company Cosco from purchasing a logistics group in Germany’s largest seaport.

The politics are only just shifting, because China has pursued a trade and investment strategy that means many German companies have become hooked on Beijing for growth.

Havrén, of Rusi, says China has developed close business ties with Germany and made a swathe of investments in infrastructure projects to gain political influence.

“China works quite a lot through German businesses,” she says.

“These big companies want to maintain relations and they have powerful lobbies that flow through to the German governments. China wants to keep Germany as the brake in Brussels. If Berlin hesitates, the EU hesitates.

“Part of German business still see China as indispensable if they want to scale.” German firms increased investment by roughly a third in the first half of this year, Havrén adds.

China also holds control over the world’s supply of rare earth minerals, which are vital for German manufacturers. When China weaponised this supply chain in a standoff with the US last year, Germany’s car industry was brought almost to a halt.

“The dependencies run so deep that China gains a lot of political leverage through these actions,” adds Havrén.

German businesses are now turning against China. In August, the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry called on Merz for a tougher stance on China.

But policymakers have made little headway. China flatly rejected European requests to commit to some form of export restraint, particularly for hybrid cars, at EU-China trade talks last week. The European Commission is discussing “safeguard” trade defence measures, prompting fear of escalation.

“I think China would likely retaliate in one way or another. There is a big risk of a trade war,” says Havrén.

“But China has so much leverage. I’m not sure the EU can afford that.”

data.title: Britain must maintain its lead to unlock energy’s holy grail
data.description:
It’s long been the “somewhere over the rainbow” promise of economic transformation that never seems to arrive. No, I’m not talking about AI, which, though already with us, has yet to prove the grandiose claims made of it.

Rather, I’m referring to nuclear fusion. This is the holy grail of energy production – the promise of limitless quantities of low-cost, carbon-free, baseload electricity.

Like the grail itself, commercialisation has thus far eluded even the world’s finest scientific minds and entrepreneurs.

But that doesn’t mean it’s still just science fiction. Lab-made fusion has already been successfully demonstrated on multiple occasions, and the science behind it is now relatively well advanced.

Yet until a few years ago, all such experimentation consumed more power than it generated, rendering it useless as an energy source.

As the old joke goes, economically viable fusion is about 30 years away, and will always be 30 years away. Harnessing the same power as the sun has proved much more difficult in practice than in theory.

In the past several years, however, there have been some very definite signs of the required breakthroughs.

And perhaps surprisingly, some of them are happening in Britain. With its history of academic excellence, the UK has always been good at this sort of stuff, but it has also been notably poor at commercialising it.

Innovative success has not translated well into economic exploitation. Rather, it is the US, and increasingly China, that tend to capitalise on what comes out of British brainpower.

Is fusion likely to suffer the same fate?

Dennis Whyte, who was this month appointed the chief executive of the UK Atomic Energy Authority – the Government body responsible for the nation’s “fusion strategy” – is determined that it should not. Formerly director of the fusion centre at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Whyte believes the UK has a unique set of capabilities that will allow it to excel in fusion’s development and commercialisation.

But first let’s talk about the potential, which to economic nerds like me is the really interesting bit.

Move over AI, the truly transformational technology coming down the road at us is not fully conscious humanoid robots but fusion.

Most economic progress is at root about energy and our ability to harness it to human purposes. At the heart of the industrial revolution, for instance, was not so much the machines themselves as the transformative power of coal.

The so-called Kardashev scale, though in some respects quack science, provides one way of charting economic advancement according to energy consumption.

Named after Nikolai Kardashev, the Soviet era astronomer, it seeks to measure progress in civilisation based entirely on the amount of energy that can be harnessed and deployed.

According to Kardashev, it’s only when humans manage to access unlimited quantities of it beyond mere Earth-bound sources that civilisation achieves its true potential.

This may or may not be an endorsement, but Elon Musk is particularly keen on the Kardashev way of thinking.

Only for him it’s about accessing the power of the sun via solar panels, battery storage and infrastructure in space. Indeed, he has dismissed pursuit of Earth-bound fusion reactors as “super dumb and farcical”.

Musk is the undisputed master of tech commercialisation, so he has to be taken seriously. Nonetheless, he should know better than anyone that progress involves, through a process of trial and error, testing the frontiers of science to virtual destruction and eventually finding a way through.

Think about it; if manmade fusion can be achieved at scale, it is likely to be a far bigger driver of productivity growth than anything AI can offer, as well as being a potential solution to any existential threat posed by climate change.

As Whyte points out, AI is a technology with unproven potential, despite the hundreds of billions of dollars being invested in it.

A lot of questions remain about its supposedly transformational powers, as last week’s wobble in AI-related stocks and shares seemed to confirm.

Nobody knows what its effect on jobs and growth might be, still less whether it is capable of generating the returns needed to justify the vast amounts being invested in it.

With energy, on the other hand, we already know what cheap power can do; fusion is moreover not just a further time-limited energy source, in the same way as a new gas field might be.

It is a forever, unlimited resource that promises to power hitherto undreamt levels of technological advancement and human progress. If it can be achieved, it truly would be a game changer, and as an economic leap forward, perhaps bigger than even the Industrial Revolution.

Interestingly, it is also complementary to the development of AI, which both has an insatiable appetite for power and whose computational skills are already helping to turbo-charge the pursuit of commercially viable fusion.

There is a developing symbiosis between the two, a mutually beneficial co-dependency which ought to help both technologies achieve their potential.

I’m no expert, so I cannot tell you if in 30 years’ time we’ll still be saying fusion is 30 years away and will always be 30 years away.

But Whyte knows as much as there is to know about fusion, and he’s never been more optimistic.

A growing number of labs and companies are successfully achieving it, including recently General Fusion Group, which has announced that its magnetised target fusion (MTF) technology has reached electron temperatures exceeding 12 million degrees Celsius, well in advance of what’s needed for fusion to take place.

The results were confirmed using the UK Atomic Energy Authority measurement techniques.

What’s more, around £10bn of private capital globally has been invested in fusion in a clear signal that commercialisation is beginning to be seen as eminently possible and even likely.

Not to be outdone, China is also chasing hard, having elevated fusion to a core strategic frontier and national infrastructure priority.

Some readers may be familiar with an Apple TV science fiction series called For All Mankind, which is based around the idea that the space race never ended.

The consequent superpower rivalry drives rapid technological progress, such that by the year 2000 space exploration and colonisation are far in advance of anything we see today.

The same rivalry already apparent between the West and China in AI is beginning to take hold in nuclear fusion, where China has a significant advantage in terms of the supply chains and manufacturing capacity needed to make fusion reactors a reality.

Still, Britain is for now very much part of the race. The UK was the first country in the world to produce nuclear power at scale for civilian use. It would be nice to think it is still capable of doing the same with fusion.

data.title: ‘China Shock 2.0’ is crushing the West
data.description:
Robot vacuum cleaners are typically less noisy than their older, hand-operated cousins. But the volume of the Chinese-made versions is not the only quiet thing. They are also stealthily taking over the world.

Dreame, a company founded in Suzhou less than a decade ago, is now said to be the world’s biggest seller of robot vacuums. Its founder, 39-year-old Yu Hao, claims to be building a $100tn (£75tn) ecosystem of smart appliances and frontier tech.

After just two years in Britain, Dreame is still a relatively small player here. Euromonitor International put the company’s UK market share at 4pc last year.

But four Chinese companies control almost half the UK market. And their cheapest products are all priced below those of SharkNinja and Dyson, which manufacture in Asia but do at least some of the brain-work in the US and Britain, respectively.

When it comes to Chinese imports, most people think first of electric vehicles (EVs), which are swarming into markets worldwide, such as Jaecoo, a brand that has become the go-to for British consumers. It is certainly the prime battlefront, with Britain under growing pressure to mimic the EU’s tariffs of up to 45pc on EVs.

Beneath these headlines, however, cut-price Chinese imports of just about any manufactured product are now sweeping into the West and challenging local businesses.

Consumers love the low prices. But companies and governments across Europe now fear that the Chinese juggernaut will hoover up Western industries and jobs, and leave the Continent utterly dependent on the whims and will of Beijing.

The timing of this “China Shock 2.0” – the first shock was the flood of low-priced toys, clothes and other manufactured goods that hit in the early 2000s – is not a coincidence. In the past few years, Beijing has unmuzzled its most potent weapon to win the export war.

Chinese factories have long enjoyed advantages such as cheap workers and raw materials, generous subsidies and massive economies of scale. But now a new wave of cheap credit – that is, loans made on concessional or non-commercial terms – has swept through the Chinese manufacturing sector, unlocking the export tsunami.

“This is probably the single biggest component of China’s industrial policy,” says Camille Boullenois, a China expert at the Rhodium Group consultancy.

“It has been the most powerful and the most influential factor shaping the economic system in China, because the entire economic system is based on credit.”

‘Everything in China is political’

Ever since China’s banks pulled back from lending to households after the spectacular property crash of 2021, they have been scrambling to find enough borrowers.

And with the Chinese government ever more focused on ramping up high-tech and advanced manufacturing, that’s where the banks have been pouring all that surplus cash.

“There’s a natural herding in the way the Chinese private sector operates. Once everybody realised that manufacturing is where the political light was shining, then capital and human talent moved into manufacturing,” says David Lubin, of the think tank Chatham House.

The banks have become the pivotal enabler of Beijing’s ambition to ensure companies, such as Dreame, dominate global markets and supply chains.

“Lending is political, because everything in China is political. And credit is a political tool,” says Leo Austin, a businessman who advises multinationals on working in China.

These dirt-cheap loans mean that, unlike their Western rivals, many Chinese companies can receive capital on tap.

“There is always cash flow available to you, and you have no short-term fear around the viability of the business, so you can afford to be incredibly aggressive,” Austin says.

This has wrought a transformation in China that is little appreciated outside its borders.

Once there were private firms and state-owned enterprises. But now most companies are a hybrid: they have a private-sector management culture, but are almost entirely funded by government-sourced equity and state-backed lending.

Austin calls this model “state-capitalised private enterprises”. The emerging Chinese high-tech giants are almost all cut from this cloth.

Chinese banks are bound by law to lend money “in accordance with the needs of the national economic and social development, and under the guidance of the industrial policies of the state”.

And they do. Beijing’s corporate debt totals about 138pc of GDP, almost double the ratio in the US. But Chinese companies’ interest costs amount to less than 1pc of turnover, compared with 5pc for their American peers.

The effect of this fresh wave of cheap credit has been immediate.

China’s domination

Between 2021 and 2024, the number of products where China accounts for more than half of global exports nearly doubled, from 192 to 315.

China’s trade surplus will again surpass $1tn this year. The surplus with both Germany and France has doubled in the past year. For the EU as a whole, it amounts to more than €1bn (£840m) a day.

Although this export surge makes China appear like a rising economic superpower, the boom in cheap credit and factory exports has a dark side.

Companies are exporting their credit-fuelled output because Chinese households, burnt by the property crash, are not spending. At home, Chinese companies are forced into painful discounting wars just to move stock.

Profitability has plummeted and one in three companies is loss-making. Without the exports, which often provide more than 40pc of revenue, many businesses would be unviable.

Yet the banks keep lending and lending. Often, they have to discount the interest rate simply because otherwise the borrower would go bust.

Instead, it is European competitors who are absorbing the blow. In Britain, some have complained to the Trade Remedies Authority (TRA), which can impose quotas or tariffs.

The TRA has sought to protect local manufacturers from cut-price Chinese imports of everything from ceramics to ironing boards, tyres and cherry-pickers.

One recent TRA ruling noted that Chinese companies “have access to preferential financing, and access to financing from institutions which implement public policy objectives or otherwise do not act independently of the state”.

The TRA added: “They have more flexibility and can adjust their business and pricing strategies to maximise their export sales and gain market share in the UK, even if they would have otherwise made negative profit margins.”

No easy answers

Given that the Government is aware of the problem, many businesses want to see it push back harder. “There are probably plenty of stones that could be unturned,” one industry veteran says.

Rhodium’s Boullenois says the same is true in Europe, where Brussels’s trade directorate is overwhelmed with business requests for protection.

“We’re protecting too few products. Our defences need to be much broader, and work much faster,” she says.

But if the EU and US protect their own markets, more of the ultra-cheap Chinese exports will simply shift to Asia, Africa and Latin America – displacing European and American rivals in those countries’ markets.

“We normally look at how much is China selling to the EU. A lot less time is spent thinking about how many EU products the Chinese manufacturers are displacing in foreign markets – and it’s huge,” says Joe Peissel, of the consultancy Trivium China.

The battle against China’s factories is on in earnest. But as long as the Chinese are backed up by the bazooka of the country’s banking system, it will be a war that the West will struggle to win.

data.title: The seasonal secret to a successful property listing
data.description:
This year’s stagnant property market has made it tough for anyone trying to sell their home.

Buyers are watching their budgets and may be more cautious about properties listed on portals for months, and one telltale sign is your photos.

Charlie Warner, from buying agent Heaton & Partners, said: “A house that is obviously out of season, such as one with scorched grass in the dead of winter or bare trees in spring, will prompt buyers to ask: ‘What’s wrong with it? Was the price wrong? Does it suffer from some blight or other?’”

As we’ve seen the back of a long, hot summer, should you focus on fresh photos and an autumnal update to secure a quicker sale, and perhaps even a higher price? Property experts share their advice.

Is it worth giving your photos a seasonal refresh?

Now that the leaves are changing colour and the nights are drawing in, it may be time to retire the photos of your home from when spring or summer was in full swing.

Mark Wheeler, the director of prime country sales at Hamptons, said: “Refreshing photography to reflect the season is generally a good idea. Autumn images are best taken before lawns get covered by falling leaves; even winter sunshine can create striking photography.”

You don’t have to revisit listing photos often. Elaine Penhaul, founder and director of home staging firm Lemon and Lime Interiors, has a simple rule of thumb.

She said: “If a property hasn’t sold within eight to 12 weeks, then it’s worth reviewing the photos. A change of season is the natural moment to do it.”

So sellers who struggle to sell their home in the next few months might want to revisit their photos in spring, when trees are in leaf and gardens look their best.

Don’t go overboard

Some property experts believe you’re better off focusing on getting the “best” photos to showcase your home.

Adam Jennings, the head of residential at Chestertons, said: “There’s no harm in making sure your property listing feels relevant to the time of year, but I wouldn’t recommend trying to make it over-seasonal.

“As we move from summer into autumn, rather than worry too much about refreshing the photography, my advice is to focus on having a strong set of high-quality images that showcase the property at its best.”

This may be a better use of time than rephotographing your home every time the seasons change.

“If the property – or its presentation – has materially changed, then it makes sense to revisit the images,” he added. “Otherwise, there’s no reason why a good set of photographs can’t work perfectly well throughout the year.”

You don’t have to replace every photo

As a compromise, consider updating just a few pictures.

“A well-staged interior can look good at any time of year, so those shots often don’t need replacing,” said Ms Penhaul. “The images that date fastest are the exterior and the garden.

“Refreshing the outside shots and main image is a quick, low-cost way to make a listing feel current again.”

This can help the listing feel fresh and authentic, without the hassle of a full reshoot.

What about rewriting the description?

Similarly, rather than starting your home description from scratch, it may be more effective to shift the emphasis to certain features throughout the seasons.

Ms Penhaul said: “As the weather cools, focus more on the appeal of the log burner, the cosy snug and good insulation. As it warms up, bring the garden, the patio and light-filled rooms forward in the description.”

Mr Wheeler also recommends tailoring the description to the time of year.

“Highlight cosy interiors, fireplaces and garaging during the colder months,” he said. “Then highlight swimming pools and outdoor entertaining spaces in spring and summer.”

But make sure the description reflects the property’s genuine strengths, rather than rewriting it just because the season has changed.

Ms Penhaul added: “Whatever you change, the photos and description must be an honest picture of the property. Buyers will see the home in person, and if it doesn’t match the listing, you’ve lost their trust before they’ve stepped through the front door.”

Does a listing which ‘suits the season’ translate into a quicker sale – or better sale price?

Some experts believe it can make a difference – though not all agree.

“I look at presentation in terms of what it costs,” said Ms Penhaul.

“Anything that makes a buyer hesitate costs you, the seller, time and money. In my view, a listing that looks ‘out of step’ with the season sends the wrong signal.”

Because it may suggest the property has been on the market for a while, it can give buyers more leverage.

Ms Penhaul added: “In the current market, where a smaller pool of committed buyers has more choice and more room to negotiate, seasonally appropriate staging can be the difference between a quick, strong sale and a property that lingers.”

But opinion is divided and other experts are less convinced that updating a listing to “suit the season” will significantly affect the outcome.

“It won’t automatically result in any quick wins,” said Mr Jennings. “There are too many other factors involved, including how the property is priced, market conditions and buyer demand.”

Mr Wheeler takes a similar view.

“It’s difficult to quantify any direct impact on sale price – or time to sell – from seasonal photography alone,” he said. “Realistic pricing remains the biggest factor.”

Other agents stress that this matters most in the current market.

Nick Leeming, the chairman of Jackson-Stops, said: “An asking price grounded in recent local sales data can attract serious buyers and create competition, giving owners the best chance of realising the full value of their property.

“Buyers may have more choice right now, but well-presented homes priced accurately are still selling quickly.”

Things to avoid at all costs

We asked the experts what they regard as a no-no:

Christmas decorations

It’s wise to avoid anything that makes the listing look tied to a particular time. “Christmas decorations are a good example,” said Mr Jennings.

“They may look attractive in December, but if the property is still on the market in January or February, the photographs can make the listing immediately feel dated.”

Mr Warner feels the same way.

He said: “My personal take on Christmas photographs is ‘Bah! Humbug!’. I think having Christmas trees in pictures may feel like a wholesome touch, but if the house doesn’t sell, you’ll just need to spend a good chunk of money retaking and restaging photographs. Many buyers find festive decorations more irksome than inviting.”

Other seasonal decorations

Ms Penhaul said: “The same goes for any seasonal decorations. Easter bunting – or a hallway full of Halloween bits and pieces – dates your photos just as quickly as tinsel.”

Rainy-day imagery

Mr Wheeler added: “One thing to steer clear of is rainy-day imagery. If the forecast is wet, reschedule the shoot.”

Why out-of-season photos aren’t always a red flag

Finally, one important caveat: an out-of-season listing isn’t necessarily a sign a property has been sitting unsold for months.

In fact, particularly for higher-value homes at the upper end of the market, where marketing often requires more planning and lead times can be longer, it’s not unusual for photos to be slightly out of season.

Mr Warner said: “It’s very common for sellers to get their house photographed in the spring or summer when the garden looks its finest; summery pictures in autumn aren’t necessarily a red flag. They can simply indicate a well-prepared seller who may even have all their documentation ready to go with the solicitor – and is ready to proceed.”

He added that buying agents often receive photos of houses that are still off the market because the seller is preparing to launch the next year.

“In these cases, you know you might have someone who has got a full legal pack waiting to go,” he said. “The key here is to understand the story behind the photos and chat with the agent before making assumptions.”

data.title: Households cut back on food before Budget
data.description:
Retail sales have fallen by more than expected before the Budget as dwindling consumer confidence prompts households to cut back on spending.

Sales slid by 0.4pc in September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), worse than economists’ expectations of a 0.1pc decline.

The drop came as households reduced spending on food, while warmer-than-expected weather also dented demand for winter clothing.

Last month’s dismal retail sales marked a significant slowdown following a 0.7pc rise in August.

The drop followed the largest monthly drop in consumer confidence since the pandemic in October, according to a closely followed survey.

Nicholas Found, of Retail Economics, said: “September marked a clear softening in retail momentum.

“Unseasonably warm weather delayed the shift into autumn wardrobes, rising fuel and household costs absorbed more of consumers’ budgets.”

Overall food sales dropped by 0.4pc in September, the ONS found, while clothing volumes sank by 0.9pc.

However, quarterly retail sales were still up by 0.7pc in the three months to September as drivers spent more on fuel.

It underscores the financial pressure on households and businesses as they brace for John Healey’s Budget.

The Chancellor is widely expected to raise taxes next week as he seeks to plug a potential £35bn shortfall in the public finances.

Oliver Vernon-Harcourt, the head of retail at Deloitte, said September’s fall in retail sales “suggests consumers are tightening their purse strings as they assess what the coming months could mean for their finances”.

He added: “The rise in inflation, fuel and energy prices, as well as falling consumer confidence, are creating a cocktail of uncertainty for many.”

Retailers have urged the Chancellor to introduce support for the sector in his maiden Budget on Oct 28. This has coincided with calls to ease cost of living pressures on households as energy bills are poised to surge this winter.

Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said: “October’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner.”

He added that consumer spending and GDP growth were likely to “grind to a halt” in the final three months of the year and the beginning of 2027 amid falling consumer confidence and a rebound in inflation.
